AstraZeneca will tap AI-focused insitro to find new targets for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and cardiomyopathies, following the Phase 3 failure of its Ionis-partnered Wainua in transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy.
AstraZeneca is offering as much as $1.5 billion to work with AI-focused insitro to find new medicines for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and cardiomyopathies.
The companies will search for new targets for drugs using insitro’s Virtual Human AI platform, which aims to identify causal disease biology. AstraZeneca will then advance the candidates through development.
Insitro will receive $40 million upfront and could see $1.46 billion in milestones, plus royalties later on, according to the company’s announcement on Thursday.
The new partnership will add to AstraZeneca’s work in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), which includes the Phase 1 anti-fibrotic asset AZD2389.
“We know that disease biology is incredibly complex and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target,” Sharon Barr, executive VP and head of BioPharmaceuticals R&D at AstraZeneca, said in a statement.
MASH had long confounded drugmakers until Madrigal Pharmaceuticals broke through, earning an FDA nod for Rezdiffra in 2024 . The achievement brought Big Pharma back into the space, with Novo , Roche and GSK striking major deals. Novo has also earned an FDA nod in the indication for its mega-blockbuster semaglutide under the Wegovy brand.
MASH
Beyond Rezdiffra: The 4 Most Promising MASH Pipelines in Play
After last year’s ‘stampede’ for FGF21 assets, the focus for the metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis space has shifted toward differentiated approaches, such as THR-β agonists and combination treatments, that seek to mirror the commercial success of Madrigal’s Rezdiffra.

·
6 min read
·

Read more
AstraZeneca previously worked with Ionis Pharmaceuticals on a MASH candidate known as AZD2693. The asset was discontinued in November 2025 after it failed to live up to expectations in a Phase 2 trial.
On the cardiomyopathy side, AstraZeneca has a deeper bench, including Ionis-partnered Wainua, which was approved in December 2023 for hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR-PN). The drug recently failed a Phase 3 trial that aimed to build a case for expansion into transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), sending shockwaves across the industry.
Earlier in Phase 1 testing, AstraZeneca is developing AZD4063 for R14del dilated cardiomyopathy.
Insitro on the other hand has shaken hands with myriad Big Pharmas such as Bristol Myers Squibb and Eli Lilly , seeking to build out a pipeline of AI-generated candidates. But the path has not been easy, with insitro laying off 22% of staff in May 2025 in an effort to extend its cash runway during a period of “macroeconomic uncertainty,” the company said at the time.

I’ve tested a lot of cargo e-bikes over the last decade-plus of reviewing electric bicycles. There are good cargo e-bikes. There are great cargo e-bikes. And then there’s Xtracycle.
More specifically, there’s the new Xtracycle Swoop ASM, which might just be a cut above every other cargo e-bike I’ve tested.
ASM stands for “Automatic Smile Machine,” and the name works on two levels. First, this thing is simply a blast to ride, whether you’re the one pedaling or one of the lucky passengers hanging out on the back. Second, it features Shimano’s automatic electronic shifting system, which appeals equally to the engineer and cyclist in me.
To see the bike in action and get my from the saddle thoughts, check out my review video below. Then keep watching for even more details about this impressive full-family cargo e-bike.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Before getting into why that automatic shifting is such a big deal, let’s run through the hardware.
The Swoop ASM is a Class 3 electric cargo bike capable of reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). It uses Shimano’s EP6 Cargo mid-drive motor paired with a 630Wh Shimano battery, with Xtracycle quoting up to 60 miles (96 km) of range. Both the motor and battery are UL-listed, so there’s nice peace of mind built right in.
The bike uses a 24-inch front wheel with a suspension fork and a smaller 20-inch rear wheel, helping keep the rear cargo deck low enough for easier loading and a lower center of gravity. Both wheels wear 2.4-inch Maxxis Metroloads, which offer a nice compromise between comfort and agility.
Stopping power comes from Tektro four-piston hydraulic disc brakes, while the drivetrain is a Shimano CUES Di2 10-speed setup.
And that drivetrain is where things get interesting.
I’ve tested automatic-shifting e-bikes before and haven’t always been impressed. Some systems leave you feeling like you’re fighting against the bike, shifting at moments you wouldn’t choose or seemingly second-guessing what you’re trying to do.
Shimano has this one dialed in.
The system seemingly just knows when I would want to shift and does it for me without getting in the way. After enough time riding the Swoop ASM, I started wishing all my bikes shifted this way.
Automatic shifting makes sense on virtually any bicycle, but it’s especially useful on a cargo bike. When you’ve got a couple of kids riding behind you, the fewer things you need to think about, the better.
There’s nothing quite like coming to a stop on a heavily loaded cargo bike, forgetting to downshift, and then discovering that you’re in a high gear while trying to get several hundred pounds of bike, rider, kids, and cargo rolling again.
The Swoop ASM solves that problem by automatically downshifting when you stop. When the light turns green, you’re already in the right gear.
It also pairs beautifully with the Shimano mid-drive motor. The torque-sensing pedal assist feels natural, and keeping the motor, drivetrain, electronic shifting, and controls within Shimano’s ecosystem makes everything feel cohesive.
Of course, carrying stuff is the entire point of a cargo bike, and Xtracycle has that part figured out too.
I used the rear setup for everything from kids to more than 100 pounds of Jackery solar generators, and the passenger corral works surprisingly well for oddly shaped cargo.
Unlike some companies that advertise an attractive base price and then make you spend hundreds more turning the bike into the family hauler you thought you were buying, Xtracycle generally includes much of that equipment in the package.
The rear passenger carrier is rated as a “2+” setup. I only managed to round up two kids for testing, but there was clearly room back there for a third if I’d been more resourceful – or simply had more nieces and nephews out of school.
Xtracycle’s accessories are also built with the same mentality as the bike itself. The enormous pannier looks like something designed to strap onto the side of a fighter jet rather than a 28 mph cargo e-bike. It is so well made that it looks like it could handle a jet stream.
This stuff feels overbuilt because Xtracycle understands that its customers use these bikes as everyday transportation.
When you’re carrying your kids, groceries, work gear, or whatever else your family can throw at the bike, overbuilt is exactly the right amount of built.
Perhaps one of the best demonstrations of the Swoop ASM’s underlying engineering is something that doesn’t appear on a spec sheet: I can ride it without my hands on the handlebars.
I don’t mean that as a recommendation for your morning school run. Rather, it demonstrates just how stable and well-designed the bike’s geometry is. Xtracycle is a real bicycle company, and it shows. The Swoop tracks beautifully and feels composed instead of giving you that vague, wandering sensation found on some long-tail cargo bikes.
It’s rare that I can actually go no-hands on a cargo bike like I can on my normal city bikes, but this one feels just as stable despite the long, stretched out frame.
There are plenty of smaller touches I appreciate, too. Integrated lighting is included, the adjustable stem helps riders dial in their cockpit position, and there’s even a dropper seat post.
That dropper is particularly useful on a cargo bike. You can ride with the saddle at the proper height for full leg extension, then drop it as you approach a stop so you can comfortably plant both feet on the ground while supporting a fully loaded bike. Start riding again, raise the saddle, and you’re immediately back in the ideal pedaling position.
Interestingly, amid all of this technology, Shimano keeps the display refreshingly simple. You get your battery level, speed, gear position, and selectable information like remaining range, odometer, and trip distance. That’s basically it.
If you want to manually control the Di2 drivetrain, shifting buttons on the right handlebar let you do that. Otherwise, just leave it in automatic and let the bike handle the gears.
The catch, unsurprisingly, is the price.
At $4,495, the Xtracycle Swoop ASM is unquestionably a premium cargo e-bike. It isn’t competing with $1,500 budget models, nor is it pretending to.
But there are also cargo e-bikes pushing $8,000, so everything is relative.
If your primary goal is spending as little as possible, there are plenty of budget cargo bikes that can get the job done. But if you want higher-end components, an excellent drivetrain, thoughtful geometry, quality accessories, and a bike designed to survive years of hard daily use, this is what paying for a premium model gets you.
And if a bike costs several times more but lasts several times longer while providing a safer, better riding experience for your family, the math starts to make a lot more sense.
Premium cargo e-bikes are a pay-to-play affair. But with the Xtracycle Swoop ASM , I can confidently say you’re getting what you pay for.
After testing more cargo e-bikes than I can count, this is one of the best examples I’ve ridden of what happens when a company doesn’t just build an electric bike with a long rack on the back, but actually understands what families need from a true car-replacing cargo e-bike.

ITF Group has released a report telling retailers to look more closely at how freight decisions affect product returns, shipping costs, and holiday-season preparation. The Missouri-based logistics provider says those issues often fall under separate departments, making it harder to link a damaged product or missed delivery appointment to the carrier decision behind it.
What’s Related
The Retail Reality Check Report argues that choosing and managing freight partners should involve more than comparing shipping rates. ITF says retailers should also track how transportation affects returns, cargo damage, and other costs that emerge after a shipment arrives.
The report cites the National Retail Federation and Happy Returns’ estimate that merchandise returns would total $849.9 billion in 2025, or 15.8% of retail sales. That research also found that 9% of returns were fraudulent. NRF
ITF’s argument centers on returns tied to shipping and handling problems. The company says damage from warehouse handling or repeated transfers between locations can eventually appear in a retailer’s returns figures without being connected to the original shipment.
RELATED STORIES: How Returns Impact Inventory Accuracy and Warehouse Confidence | Turning Returns Into Revenue: Mastering Reverse Logistics at Scale
Hiding the blame for higher prices
“We've accepted a false premise in this industry; we talk about returns as if they're a customer service issue, something e-commerce has to deal with,” said Sam Agyemang, ITF Group’s vice president of business development. “In reality, many of those returns are symptoms of an execution failure. And it's always upstream.”
The report argues that a lower freight rate can bring additional costs when a carrier misses an appointment or damages merchandise. Those expenses may appear in another department’s budget, making the initial shipping discount look more valuable than it ultimately was.
ITF recommends that retailers examine transportation performance alongside return rates. That means looking beyond whether a truck arrived on time to understand what happened to the merchandise along the way.
Checking carriers before peak season
The report closes with five questions for retail finance, merchandising, and operations teams heading into the fourth quarter. They cover visibility into return rates, carrier risk scoring, broker liability, ongoing carrier checks, and readiness for peak shipping demand.
ITF also points to its own operations as an example of its approach. The company reports a 98% on-time record, moves more than 100,000 loads annually through its trucking and brokerage businesses and has approximately 65,000 vetted carriers.
According to ITF, enhanced fraud-prevention and turnaround controls have reduced fraud-related incidents and exposure by roughly 90%. The company also reports an in-transit damage rate of approximately 0.004%.
For retailers reviewing their freight partners, the report’s main recommendation is to connect shipping performance with what happens after delivery.
“A question every shipper should ask themselves is how many companies measure transportation success only by on-time delivery, and never measure how transportation affects return rates,” said Sam Burkhan, CEO of ITF Group.

A new biotech co-founded by Paul Stoffels has formed to take on the CAR T cell assets of Galapagos almost a year after the company—now known as Lakefront Biotherapeutics—abandoned them.
The abandoned CAR T cell therapies of Galapagos have found a new home under the very CEO who placed them front and center at the company: Paul Stoffels. The former Johnson & Johnson executive has formed a new biotech in Belgium called Armed Cell Therapeutics to take on the project, offering just under $240 million in biobucks to secure the assets from Galapagos, now known as Lakefront Biotherapeutics.
It’s a been a long and winding tale for the cell therapies, Stoffels and Lakefront. But the licensing deal, announced Wednesday , brings an end to at least one significant chapter.
In early 2025, then-Galapagos announced a plan to split into two businesses: one taking the cell therapy assets and another with a deep war chest to hunt down new assets to develop. The company at the time was helmed by Stoffels, who had promised a five-year turnaround when he took the job in 2022. He had carefully curated Galapagos’ cell therapy portfolio through a series of acquisitions.
But Stoffels was ousted in spring 2025 to make way for Henry Gosebruch, who had been running the proposed spinout that was hunting for new assets.
Mergers & acquisitions
JPM26: Galapagos’ New CEO Is Here To Finally Turn the Ship Around
Henry Gosebruch, who has $3.5 billion in capital to deploy, is thinking broad as he steers the decades-old biotech out of years of turmoil.
January 19, 2026
·
4 min read
·
Annalee Armstrong
Read more
Under this new leadership, the cell therapy programs were officially abandoned in October 2025 as Gosebruch changed directions. In May 2026, the company rebranded to Lakefront Biotherapeutics.
In March, the company and partner Gilead Sciences acquired Ouro Medicines for $2.1 billion, securing a pipeline of T cell engager therapies for autoimmune diseases. The lead asset from the transaction is gamgertamig, which Lakefront is now developing in Phase 1/2 trials for autoimmune bullous diseases, autoimmune cytopenia and seropositive autoimmune diseases.
That left the cell therapy programs, which Lakefront had no intention of developing. Gosebruch, speaking to BioSpace in January, said that the programs would have required a massive investment to advance the technology far enough to tap into a very competitive market—one that is led in part by Gilead. Gosebruch said at the time that no one had come forward to buy the assets.
But the CEO did say that Stoffels was very invested in the programs. “Paul for many, many years and I have a lot of respect, but he was very, very focused on cell therapy,” Gosebruch explained. “That was sort of his mission, to bring this set of programs to patients. And I think, given how focused he was on that particular mission, I think he was not focused on opening up to other potential opportunities.”
Now, Stoffels has found a way to continue his work on the cell therapies via Armed. Stoffels founded the company with John Mellors, who previously led cell therapy discovery at Galapagos, and Peter Verhaeghe, a managing partner at Belgian law firm VVGB Advocaten/Avocats.
Armed’s lead programs—still in preclinical research—will focus on non-Hodgkin lymphoma and small cell lung cancer. The programs originated from AboundBio, which was one of the companies purchased by Galapagos during Stoffels’ tenure.
The new company offered Lakefront about $9 million upfront for the early-stage programs and $230 million on the backend in milestones, plus royalties.
“I’m pleased we were able to complete this sale of the early-stage cell therapy programs as it provides a path to continue to advance these assets on behalf of patients,” said Sooin Kwon, chief business officer at Lakefront. “Additionally, it offers Lakefront shareholders the opportunity to benefit from their potential future progress by the experienced team at Armed Cell Therapeutics.”
At the new company, Stoffels will yield the CEO chair to Willemijn Kremer after serving in the role on an interim basis, according to a separate Thursday press release from Armed. While the company is headquartered in Belgium, it will have operations in the Netherlands, R&D work in Pittsburgh and early development activities in Europe, Asia and the U.S.
Kremer also joins from Galapagos, where she served as VP of corporate development for cell therapy and chief of staff.

After a 12-month period that saw the Belgian biotech consider a spinout, swap out CEOs, and enter a three-way acquisition agreement involving Ouro Medicines, Galapagos now has a new moniker.

Stoffels will chair Armed’s board, Verhaeghe will serve as a board member and Mellors will be chief scientific officer and board member.
“This acquisition gives us a strong scientific starting point and a team that knows these programs inside out,” Verhaeghe said in a Wednesday release from Armed.
Both Stoffels and Mellors emphasized that the CAR T cell therapy programs are highly differentiated, offering a chance to prevent relapse. Unlike traditional CAR T therapies, the assets have additional payloads to go after multiple targets, offering additional shots on goal to maintain anti-tumor activity.
“We have differentiated science and a team with deep experience in this field,” Stoffels said in a prepared statement. “Our focus now is to bring these programs to the clinic with speed and scientific rigor.”

source_document.body:
A Tesla crossed the grass median of Route 55 in New Jersey, hit a tree, slid into oncoming traffic, and struck an SUV head-on. The SUV’s driver, 68-year-old Phillip Eastman, was killed.
Police reported it as a driver who lost control. What they didn’t say, and likely didn’t know, is that Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says the car’s driver-assist system was engaged. This is part of an ongoing Electrek investigation matching reported crashes to Tesla’s redacted NHTSA data.
What happened on Route 55
Around 8:31 a.m. on Saturday, August 22, 2026, a Tesla was heading south on Route 55 in Vineland, in Cumberland County, near milepost 34.6. The driver lost control, ran off the left side of the road, crossed the grass median, struck a tree, and continued into the northbound lanes, where the car hit a northbound Chevrolet SUV, according to the New Jersey State Police.
The SUV’s driver, Phillip “Phil” Eastman, 68, of Springfield, Pennsylvania , was killed. The Tesla’s driver and a passenger in the Chevrolet were hurt and taken to a hospital with moderate injuries.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Eastman had just been sworn in as a Springfield School District board member, and he spent nearly three decades coaching youth and high school ice hockey, including 17 years as the varsity head coach at Springfield High. His death was widely covered in the Philadelphia area.
And in all of it, no report mentioned Autopilot, “Full Self-Driving,” or any driver-assist system. The crash was told as a driver who lost control of his car.
What Tesla told the federal government
Under a NHTSA Standing General Order, automakers must report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed. Tesla filed a report on this crash.
In it, Tesla identifies the car as a 2021 Model Y and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged” — meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was active. It lists the New Jersey State Police as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from the media.
Then it redacts the fields that would explain what the car did: the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area. All blacked out as “confidential business information,” the same redactions Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports .
What the data doesn’t settle
We want to be precise about what this does and doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds of impact” is the reporting trigger, not proof the system was steering when the car crossed the median. The driver may have been overriding it. And Tesla redacted the software version, so there’s no telling whether this was basic Autopilot or FSD.
Two more gaps are worth flagging. Tesla logs a pre-crash speed of just 37 mph, low for a freeway, which is more likely a single telematics snapshot from the pre-crash window than the speed at which the car left the road. And on this report Tesla checks only that it holds the car’s telematics, not the event-data recorder or video, so there may be less onboard evidence here than in other cases.
What is not in doubt is the one fact the public never got: a driver-assist system was on in a car that crossed a highway median and killed a man. Everything that would explain how is sealed.
Why we keep doing this
This is the pattern the investigation keeps surfacing, and it’s why the redaction matters. Tesla is, more than ever, pushing owners to treat a Level 2 driver-assistance system as if it drives itself. It sells the software as “Full Self-Driving,” Elon Musk keeps promising unsupervised autonomy is close, and the branding invites drivers to trust the car.
But it is still Level 2. The human is driving and responsible at all times, and Tesla’s own actions confirm it: consumer FSD still requires supervision, and its robotaxi service is a small, closely watched fleet. At the moment Tesla is telling owners to trust the car, it hides the records that would show how the system behaves when things go wrong, and a man coaching kids’ hockey one season is a name in a sealed federal file the next.
How we matched it, and why it’s notable: Electrek flagged this crash weeks ago, from the news, as a fatal Tesla wreck that had no corresponding entry in the federal data, and no public mention of driver-assist. The latest NHTSA release added it, flagged as a fatality with the system verified engaged. The record is unredacted on location (Vineland), state, vehicle (2021 Model Y), the fatality, and the month, and the incident time Tesla logged, 12:29 UTC, converts to about 8:29 a.m. local, within two minutes of the 8:31 a.m. police reported. It’s the same crash. Electrek has reached out to the New Jersey State Police for the crash report and the vehicle data, and asked whether investigators received Tesla’s raw telemetry or only Tesla’s own interpretation of it.
Electrek’s Take
Strip the redaction away and this is a Tesla, running its driver-assist software, that crossed a median and killed a school board member in the oncoming lane. Leave it in place, as Tesla did, and it’s a driver who “lost control.” Those are very different stories, and the public got the one that leaves Tesla out of it.
We’re careful here. The system being on doesn’t prove it caused the crash, the driver may have been overriding it, and we don’t even know if it was Autopilot or FSD. That is exactly the problem. Tesla knows all of it. It has the telematics, it filed the report confirming the system was engaged, and it decided that what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret, down to which software was running. Phillip Eastman’s family, and the troopers still investigating, deserve the full account, not a redacted one.
Tesla is already under NHTSA investigation over how it reports these crashes. We’ll keep matching them, one by one, until the record is whole.

Chinese Regulators Propose New Car Design Rules That Make a Whole Lot of Sense
19 photos
Photo: Xiaomi
Ever had a moment when you needed the wipers or demister, and the only way to turn either of them on was to use touch controls? Chinese regulators have had enough of that distracting nonsense. A new draft published by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology would force automakers to keep physical controls for many vital functions, ban folding and flexible displays, and make them prove new designs can actually survive a year of real-world abuse.
Published on the MIIT's website on October 10, comments on the new draft are open through November 10. Per said proposal, displays would face assessments for extreme weather reliability, crash safety, and - most importantly - distraction. China is also planning to ban flexible or foldable in-vehicle displays, which are completely nonsensical when you think about it from a practical standpoint.
The physical controls requirement is the part resonating most with me and pretty much everyone who understands what muscle memory stands for in this context. Lights, wipers, and demisting/defrosting controls have to be physical under this proposal. Touch- and pressure-sensitive buttons would face checks for accidental operation and clear feedback.
Then there are emergency escape controls, emergency braking controls, and the drive system's power cut-off, which are required to embrace physical hardware with conspicuous markings to boot. So far, the Chinese regulators are as sensible as you would expect them to be.
Regulators are targeting voice control as well. If the vehicle is being driven, passengers would not be allowed to directly operate the headlights or any other vital function through voice control. Gesture control and similar interfaces are targeted as well. The wording of the draft clearly targets non-driving occupants.
Photo: Xiaomi Carmakers would also have to assess recognition, command confirmation, and protection against unintended operation. The seating provisions would keep zero-gravity and similar automotive seat designs from reclining, swiveling, and everything in between while driving. Door handles receive an explicit prohibition of completely hidden designs, alongside requirements for mechanical redundancy and sufficient hand-operating space.
Soft-close doors would need anti-pinch protection and manual opening after a malfunction or power loss. The Chinese draft further poses the question of what happens after mud or water obstructs rearview cameras that feed into camera-only mirrors. In other words, the Polestar 4 and similar vehicles are targeted by this very sensible question. That's not all, though.
Integrated lamps, protruding lights, and bumpers that hide fragile componentry like air suspension reservoirs would require repair cost assessments. Combining functions might be impressive from an engineering standpoint, but the proposed review is focused on material reliability and how that complexity affects repair costs. Exterior message displays would need content oversight as well.

Tesla’s Senior Manager of Cybercab General Assembly at Gigafactory Texas, Jody Kerns, is leaving the company to become Rivian’s Director of General Assembly for the R2 in Normal, Illinois.
He’s the second Cybercab launch leader to leave Tesla this year. The head of Cybercab new product introduction walked out in April, before the vehicle ever carried a paying passenger.
From Cybercab to R2
Kerns announced the move in a LinkedIn post this week, thanking his Tesla team for everything “from the WEOL project to the launch of the Cyber Cab.”
His profile shows he joined Tesla in January 2024 as an end-of-line manager and took over Cybercab general assembly in Austin in February 2026. That’s the same month Tesla rolled the first steering-wheel-less Cybercab off the line , so he ran final assembly through the entire ramp to commercial service.

At Rivian, he’ll do the same job on the R2. He described the goal as making the R2 “the best electric SUV in the market.”
Kerns isn’t a Silicon Valley hire. He spent 14 years at Volkswagen of America, ending as Director of Assembly from 2021 to 2024, where his profile says he managed about 1,200 people and integrated the ID.4 into a line already building two other models. That’s the Chattanooga plant. Before that, he spent four years in Toyota’s paint shops.
So Rivian is getting someone who has slotted a new EV into a running factory and launched a brand new vehicle from scratch. That’s exactly the R2 problem.
The second Cybercab leader out the door
Kerns’ departure follows Michael So, who was Tesla’s Head of Cybercab NPI from September 2024 to April 2026. So was Giga Texas employee #1 in 2021, helped launch the Model Y and Cybertruck there, and lists the Cybercab’s “unboxed” manufacturing process, brake-by-wire, and butterfly doors among the things he launched.
He left in May to become VP of Product Engineering at Aalo Atomics, a nuclear reactor startup also based in Austin. Under Kerns’ post, So wrote that he “wouldn’t want to launch Cybercab with anyone else.”
The timing isn’t great for Tesla. Commercial Cybercab rides started in Austin on September 3, and NHTSA hit Tesla with a Special Order a week later demanding proof, under oath, that a car with no steering wheel or brake pedal meets federal safety standards. NHTSA now estimates the 2026 Robotaxi fleet, Model Y and Cybercab combined, at about 1,000 vehicles.

Jeff Bezos-backed electric truck startup Slate Auto opened the doors to its first-ever brick-and-mortar “experience center” in Chicago’s Near West Side, offering midwest fleet buyers and automotive journalists (Hi!) their first real, up-close look at what promises to be the most affordable new vehicle in America .
It’s true even in the tight, urban jungle of Chicago: Illinois loves trucks. Increasingly, Illinois seems to love EVs , too – so it makes sense that a new electric truck startup like Slate would choose Chicago as the home of its first-ever Slate experience center.
Familiar territory
1053 W Grand AVE; image by the author.
The covers are off of the renovations at the old Tesla store on Grand, revealing that the new tenants are, in fact, Slate – and that makes total sense. Not only was the building already laid out for a small showroom, garage and retail space, it was also wired for NACS EV charging. Combine those logistical advantages with the location’s proven track record of getting the EV-curious behind the wheel, and the spot was a no-brainer.
Once potential customers get inside the Slate, they’ll be met with a solid, heavily-sprung door handle that feels expensive, and clicks, pulls, and snaps back with authority. The same is true of the chonky steering wheel, manual seat adjusters, tailgate latch, and charge port cover. The center console, too, despite looking like it was made of JC Whitney -spec shiny plastic, didn’t budge, and felt like it might be made of basalt, rather than plastic. Just about everything you touch, in other words, delivers reassuring haptics that shout, rather than whisper: Slate may be inexpensive, but it’s not cheap !
Advertisement - scroll for more content
They got the important bits right
That idea carried on through my test ride (I wasn’t allowed to drive), which was quiet, smooth, free of squeaks and rattles on Chicago’s perpetually under construction roads, and felt more than quick enough from where I was sitting.
It was an impressive showing, and my conversation with some of Slate’s tech people about using the same fasteners throughout the vehicle whenever possible gave me a brief glimpse into what is sure to be an absolutely bananas, 3d-printed tuner culture around this thing … but that’s still speculative, and Slate’s overall success is far from a sure thing .
That said, Slate Auto is starting to feel really, really real – and if you’re in Chicago, you now have the chance to see just how real it is for yourself.

source_document.body:
If your trucks have been running the same heavy-duty diesel engine oil since roughly 2017, whether you manage a hundred-truck fleet, run a small operation of a few units, or own the one truck you drive yourself, that oil is about to be replaced by something new, because the American Petroleum Institute is rolling out a fresh engine oil category called PC-12 that takes effect at the start of January 2027, and everybody who buys oil, specs it for a fleet, or just has it poured in at a shop needs to understand what is changing before it shows up at the next service interval.
This is not a marketing refresh or a new label on the same jug. It is a genuine category change, the kind the industry only goes through about once a decade. The last one landed in 2016. Before that, 2006. So if it feels like you have been buying the same oil forever, that is because, in category terms, you nearly have. What is coming in January is a real shift in how these oils are formulated, what they are certified to do, and in one important case, which engines they are even allowed to go into.
If you sit on the leadership side of a carrier, this belongs on your radar now as a procurement, budgeting, and equipment-planning item rather than a shop-floor detail to delegate and forget. The oil your fleet buys in bulk, the specs your maintenance team writes, the warranty language on the trucks you are ordering for 2027 , and the fuel-economy case behind your next tractor purchase all run through this change. For the owner-operator, it is the same set of decisions at a smaller scale, made at the parts counter instead of in a supply contract. Either way the move is the same, which is to understand it before January rather than scramble after it.
We spent time digging into this one, including sitting through a technical briefing from the people who formulate these products, and we want to be upfront about something. We are not oil chemists. What follows is our best effort to translate a very technical subject into plain language a working carrier can actually use. Where the data comes from a manufacturer, we will say so, because a company presenting its own test results is not the same thing as an independent verdict, and you deserve to know the difference.
What Is Actually Changing
Right now, the two heavy-duty diesel oil categories you deal with are CK-4 and FA-4. CK-4 is the workhorse. It is the backward-compatible oil that goes into just about everything, old trucks and new. FA-4 was the lower-viscosity, fuel-economy option built for newer engines that could handle it.
PC-12 replaces both of them, and here is the part that trips people up. PC-12 is not a single oil. It splits into two separate categories, and the difference between them matters a great deal depending on what you run.
The first is API CL-4. Think of this as the direct successor to CK-4. It is backward compatible, which means it is designed to go into the engines you already own, old and new alike. If you have a 2015 truck or a 2024 truck, CL-4 is built to cover it. It carries on in the same familiar grades you buy today, the 15W-40, 10W-30, and 5W-30 that fill most fleet shelves. For the vast majority of the trucks on the road today, this is the category you will be buying.
The second is API FB-4. This is the low-viscosity, fuel-economy category, and this is the one to pay attention to, because FB-4 is not backward compatible. It is engineered for the model-year 2027 and newer engines that are being designed around it. You cannot simply pour FB-4 into your current truck to chase better fuel mileage. The engine has to be built for it. Putting it in the wrong engine is not a shortcut to savings, it is a mistake that can cost you a lot more than the few cents per mile you were hoping to pick up.
Part of what makes FB-4 different is viscosity. The new category introduces a thinner grade, the XW-20 family, meaning 0W-20 and 5W-20 oils. Those are noticeably thinner than the 10W-30 and 15W-40 oils most fleets run now, and that thinness is where the fuel economy comes from.
Why This Is Happening Now
None of this is happening because the oil companies got bored. It is being driven by emissions rules and by the engine makers themselves.
The model-year 2027 emissions and greenhouse-gas standards are pushing engine manufacturers to build cleaner, more efficient diesel engines, and those engines place new demands on the oil. These are not small targets. The new engines are being designed to cut nitrogen-oxide emissions by roughly 80 percent and particulate emissions by about half compared to what came before, and hitting numbers like that means tighter-running, hotter, more tightly sealed engines that are far less forgiving of an oil that cannot keep up. The engine builders, working through their trade group, formally asked the industry to develop a new oil category that could match. In other words, the engines are changing first, and the oil is being built to keep pace.
A thinner oil cuts the energy an engine spends just moving its own lubricant around. One of the formulators put it in terms anybody can picture. Moving honey around takes effort. Moving water takes almost none. Thinner oil behaves more like the water in that comparison, so the engine burns less fuel fighting its own oil. That is the fuel-economy logic behind the XW-20 grades and the FB-4 category.
But thinner oil and cleaner-burning engines come with a catch, and this is where the real engineering happens. A thinner film has less physical cushion between moving metal parts, so the oil has to work harder chemically to protect against wear. On top of that, the new category tightens the limits on sulfated ash, phosphorus, and sulfur, the group the industry calls SAPS, the chemistry that can clog up the aftertreatment systems, the DPF and SCR hardware, that keep these trucks legal. Lower levels of that chemistry mean longer aftertreatment life and better emissions performance, but some of those same ingredients were also doing double duty protecting your engine from wear.
To make sure the new oils actually hold up, the category adds a new engine test built specifically to torture the parts that thinner oil puts at risk. It is a cylinder liner scuffing test, and its whole purpose is to force an engine toward the kind of catastrophic liner-and-ring wear that a weak oil would allow. To pass, an oil has to survive a set number of hours under that abuse. It is a meaningful addition, because it targets exactly the failure mode operators worry about when they hear the word thinner.
The Wear Question, And Why It Matters To You
Here is the concern that comes up in every shop and every drivers’ lounge the moment this subject gets raised. If they are pulling out the chemistry that protects my engine, is my engine going to wear out faster?
It is a fair question, and the honest answer is that it deserves scrutiny rather than a reflexive yes or no.
The chemistry in question is mostly a compound built around zinc and phosphorus, the additives long associated with anti-wear protection. Under the old CK-4 oils, phosphorus levels commonly ran around 1,200 parts per million. Under the new CL-4 category, the ceiling drops to 800 parts per million, with zinc coming down alongside it. That is a real reduction, not a rounding error, and it is the reason some engine makers have been openly cautious about whether wear protection will hold.
The formulators argue that it will, and they have put data behind that argument. According to the manufacturer we heard from, the lower phosphorus levels are being offset by supplemental anti-wear additives, and their field testing has not shown a wear penalty. That company reported roughly 15 million miles of documented field-trial running across a wide mix of operations, from long-haul over-the-road fleets to coal-hauling heavy haul, mining equipment, farm equipment, diesel pickups, local delivery, and even city taxis.
The most striking piece of evidence they shared came from teardowns on two high-mileage Detroit Diesel DD15 engines running out of a North Carolina fleet. Both trucks were past 700,000 miles. Both had spent their first stretch on the older CK-4 oil and then switched over to the new PC-12 chemistry, accumulating well over half their total miles on the new formulation. When the engines were pulled apart and inspected, the manufacturer described the parts as extremely clean and showed a main bearing with essentially no measurable wear after 700,000 miles.
That is a genuinely impressive result, and it is worth taking seriously. It is also, and we want to be clear about this, the oil company’s own data presented to make the case for its own product. Independent, long-term field verification across many brands and many engines is what ultimately settles a question like this, and that evidence accumulates over years, not months. The early picture the manufacturer paints is reassuring. It is not the same as a neutral referee blowing the whistle. Both of those things can be true at once, and a smart operator holds both in mind.
What This Means For Your Operation
Strip away the chemistry and here is what actually lands on your desk, whether that desk belongs to a fleet maintenance manager spec’ing oil for dozens of trucks or an owner-operator standing at a parts counter.
Know your category. For the trucks you own today, CL-4 is your oil. It is the backward-compatible successor to CK-4, and it is built to protect the engines already in your fleet. When CK-4 starts disappearing from shelves, CL-4 is what replaces it for your existing equipment, and the transition for those trucks is designed to be seamless.
Do not put FB-4 in an engine that was not built for it. This is the single most important thing to take away. FB-4 is the thin, fuel-saving oil, and it only belongs in the model-year 2027 and newer engines engineered around it. The fuel savings are real on those new engines. Chasing them in your current truck by buying the thinner oil is not a clever hack, it is a path to accelerated wear and potential engine damage. If a price difference or a fuel-economy pitch ever tempts you toward FB-4 for an older truck, that is the moment to stop and check your engine maker’s specification.
Expect the switch itself to be smooth for most trucks. Based on the field data, the vast majority of trucks on the road can move from CK-4 to CL-4 without drama. The oils are built to be compatible with your existing drain intervals and operating conditions. You are not looking at a forced engine change or a new maintenance regimen, you are looking at a different jug on the shelf that does the same job for your current equipment.
Keep buying to your OEM spec and keep your documentation. This matters more than ever during a category change. Your engine manufacturer will tell you exactly which category and viscosity your warranty requires. Buy to that spec, keep your receipts and your oil-analysis records, and you protect both your engine and your warranty position if a dispute ever comes up. For a fleet running oil analysis programs, this is also the window to watch your wear-metal trends closely through the transition, because your own used-oil data is the most honest feedback you will ever get on how a new oil is treating your specific engines in your specific duty cycle.
Think about the fuel-economy math honestly. For fleets taking delivery of model-year 2027 and newer trucks, FB-4 and the XW-20 grades are where the fuel savings live, and across a large fleet those cents per mile add up to real money over a year. That is a legitimate reason to pay attention to the new category as you cycle in new equipment. Just remember that the savings are tied to the new engines, not to the oil by itself, and that fuel surcharge recovery and your cost-per-mile picture should factor into how you value that gain. A half-cent-per-mile fuel improvement means one thing to a fleet turning over tractors every three years and something very different to an operator keeping a paid-off truck for the long haul.
Why It Matters
PC-12 is the biggest change to heavy-duty diesel oil in about ten years, and the core of it is simple. Your current trucks move to CL-4, built to protect them just like the CK-4 you run now, while your new 2027-and-later trucks open the door to FB-4, the thinner fuel-saving oil that does not belong in anything older. You do not need to panic or stockpile old oil, you need to know which category each truck takes and keep buying to the spec your engine maker publishes.
That is what makes this worth your attention now rather than in January. The one mistake that will actually hurt, pouring the thin FB-4 into an engine built for CL-4, can turn a routine oil purchase into a major repair bill, and the carriers and owner-operators who learn the two-category split today will treat the switch as a non-event while the ones who wait will be making the call under pressure at the counter with the wrong information.
This article draws on a technical briefing from Shell Rotella’s formulation team at the Shell Technology Center Houston, along with published American Petroleum Institute category information and emissions-standard guidance from the Environmental Protection Agency and the Truck and Engine Manufacturers Association. Field-performance and teardown figures are as presented by the manufacturer and reflect its own testing rather than independent verification.

FedEx Corp. has introduced an online portal for pharmaceutical and life sciences companies to simplify booking and management of temperature-controlled parcel shipments in Europe.
Medicines, vaccines, biologics and other critical healthcare products typically follow a separate booking process because they require specialized, value-added services beyond a standard parcel. That process includes providing a validated temperature-controlled package as part of the FedEx Temp-Assure Advantage (FTAA) service, with packaging supplied and managed through specialized fulfillment centers.
Before the new FTAA portal, arranging these services often involved multiple steps and coordination between the customer, fulfillment center, and transportation network. The new portal digitizes and streamlines the process by enabling customers to manage onboarding, ordering of pre-conditioned packaging, shipment scheduling and returns through a single online platform.
Temperature-controlled healthcare logistics has traditionally involved a significant degree of manual coordination across the industry. By bringing key steps into a single digital workflow, the FTAA portal helps simplify the process, improve visibility and reduce administrative effort for customers, FedEx said in a news release on Tuesday.
The platform is available for pharmaceutical manufacturers, biotech companies and clinical trial operators for non-freight, intra-European and domestic service in 26 markets in time for the peak shipping season. It applies to air and road shipments, and is expected to help to improve efficiency and control over temperature-sensitive goods during a period of increased demand.
Why It Matters: As demand grows for biologics, specialty medicines and vaccines, maintaining strict temperature control is critical to ensuring product efficacy and patient safety. FedEx earlier this year created a new interdisciplinary life sciences unit , part of the company’s increased strategic focus on healthcare logistics.
FedEx Temp-Assure Advantage is a service designed to support the exacting requirements of the pharmaceutical and life sciences industries. It combines qualified packaging, tested in the FedEx Packaging lab, with the company’s integrated European transportation network and pharma-certified distribution facilities to help maintain temperature integrity for products requiring frozen, refrigerated or cool temperatures during transit of up to 96 hours, or more. It also utilizes reusable containers to help reduce waste.

Police departments have been increasingly turning to electric bicycles as a new tool for patrols, and in at least some cases, federal money is helping put officers in the saddle.
The latest example comes from Clinton, where the local Police Department and County Sheriff’s Office recently received five all-terrain e-bikes for use in areas that officers previously had to patrol on foot.
The Recon Power Bikes include three units for the Police Department, including one designated for its mental health co-responder, along with two bikes for the Sheriff’s Office. The bikes and additional equipment were fully funded through the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant.
That program is one of the primary sources of federal criminal justice funding distributed to state and local governments, and in this case, some of that money is being used to give officers a new form of electric transportation.

The e-bikes have already been in service for a couple of weeks. With speeds of up to 20 mph (32 km/h) and a claimed range of up to 50 miles (80 km), they can cover significantly more ground than officers on foot or pedal bikes while still accessing trails, parks, and other areas where patrol cars aren’t particularly useful.
E-bikes are proving popular with police departments, including these BULLS e-bikes serving the LAPD
It’s part of a broader trend we’ve been watching as police departments increasingly adopt e-bikes for everything from trail patrols to downtown policing and community engagement.
The appeal isn’t hard to understand. Compared to patrol cars and motorcycles, e-bikes are relatively inexpensive to purchase and operate. They don’t require gasoline, can squeeze through areas inaccessible to larger vehicles, and allow officers to cover considerably more ground than traditional bicycle or foot patrols.
They can also make police more approachable. An officer rolling slowly through a park or downtown area on a bicycle is much easier to interact with than one sitting behind the windows of a patrol car.
E-bikes obviously aren’t replacing police cruisers anytime soon, but they don’t need to. They’re increasingly filling the sizable gap between foot patrols and full-sized vehicles.
And with federal grant money potentially covering the entire cost, it’s not hard to see why more departments are giving electric two-wheelers a try.

SHIPPENSBURG, Pa. — Volvo Trucks wants 15% of the North American heavy-truck market. Peter Voorhoeve, president of Volvo Trucks North America, says that goal counts on vocational trucks, a segment where Volvo has held a low single-digit share.
Voorhoeve runs the North American arm of a brand with a large construction-truck business abroad. Volvo’s cab-over FMX holds about 30% of the vocational market in both Europe and Brazil, he said in a keynote at Volvo Construction Equipment’s Customer Center. The X marks Volvo’s vocational trucks worldwide: the FMX sits beside the long-haul FH and regional FM in cab-over markets, as the VNX now sits beside the VNL and VNR in North America.
The VNX, unveiled Wednesday , is the third truck on a shared North American platform after the long-haul VNL and regional-haul VNR. Volvo’s largest North American investment program includes more than $2 billion in new products , reported earlier in March. Volvo puts the total, including manufacturing, at $3 billion.
The three trucks share a chassis and electrical architecture, Voorhoeve said in an interview with FreightWaves, while each gets its own cab.
“When we then decided to put in a two-billion-dollar investment program platform, of course we need the whole market,” he said. “So let’s make now a platform where we can do the long haul, the regional haul, and the vocational.”
Voorhoeve put Volvo’s share of vocational at 2% to 3% in his keynote.
“Twenty-five percent, or anyway between twenty-five and thirty percent, is vocational—construction—which is a fairly stable segment,” he told FreightWaves. “So we developed products for the long haul, which is half of the market. We developed products for regional, which is a quarter of the market. And then we had a limited presence in vocational.”
Why Volvo built long haul first
Length rules explain the order. European rules cap the length of the whole tractor-trailer, Voorhoeve said, so builders put the driver on top of the engine to leave more room for payload. That produced the cab-over trucks Volvo sells across most of the world.
“Here in the US, the trailer length is regulated, but the combination length is not regulated,” he said. “So you can make a much longer tractor.”
Federal rules bar states from setting an overall length limit on tractor-semitrailer combinations on the National Network of truck routes. U.S. hauls also run longer, and Voorhoeve pointed to a mail hauler that runs Volvo trucks between Miami and Los Angeles every day.
“That’s two and a half, three days, and they do the desert,” he said. “So you need to be able to live in your truck.”
When Volvo came to the U.S., it bought the White factory and built White trucks under the Volvo logo for 10 years, Voorhoeve said. It launched the VNL in 1996 with what he called the first integrated sleeper in the North American market. The VHD followed in 2000 as Volvo’s construction truck, which Voorhoeve called a great truck with fairly limited applications.
Infrastructure and data centers
Vocational demand has run a little stronger than the rest of the market in recent years, Voorhoeve said, which he credited to the bipartisan infrastructure law and its spending on bridges, airports and highways.
Voorhoeve expects data center construction to carry that strength forward.
“Then we saw it coming back to normal a little bit, but of course now, with the whole data center boom, we will see a continuation of strength in that segment,” he said. “Will it explode? That I don’t really believe, but I think it will remain a very strong segment.”
Volvo is aiming the VNX at agriculture, municipalities, concrete, construction and roll-on/roll-off work, he said.
The overall market is less predictable. In his keynote, Voorhoeve described a North American truck market that can swing from 220,000 trucks a year to 300,000 and back, a range he said is hard to staff a factory around.
Trucks sold alongside construction equipment
Volvo’s other edge sits inside the same group. Volvo Construction Equipment sells machines into the job sites where VNX customers will haul to and from the pit.
“If you have a Volvo Construction Equipment loader, why wouldn’t you look at the Volvo trucks VNX?” Voorhoeve said.
The two businesses share a back office, which Voorhoeve said makes it easier to do business with customers. In-house financing can put a wheel loader and a truck in the same contract. The group’s U.S. parts warehouses stock both construction equipment and truck parts, and both businesses draw engine technology from the Volvo Group’s global powertrain division.
The VNX design drew on the same relationship. Voorhoeve said in his keynote that Volvo combined its global vocational experience with Volvo CE’s knowledge of how a job site runs, including how wheel loaders and trucks work together.
Vocational customers do not all buy the same way, he said. Some specialize in heavy haul, moving equipment or even houses, and only some own both machines and trucks.
“Some operators have both the yellow machines and the trucks, and some don’t,” Voorhoeve said. “But we have now the opportunity at least to combine there where necessary if the customer asks for that.”
The 15% target
Volvo set the goal at the Volvo Group’s November 2024 Capital Markets Day , held at the Volvo Trucks Customer Center in Dublin, Va., Voorhoeve said. Volvo’s North American heavy-duty market share was 8.4% in 2025, down from 9% in 2024, according to the Volvo Group’s fourth-quarter 2025 report .
He declined to put a number on where Volvo’s vocational share will be in a year.
“Let’s see where we end up,” he said. Volvo, he said, was “fairly firm that we believe that with Volvo Trucks we should be able to get to fifteen percent market share, and that combines long haul, regional haul, and vocational.”
Asked whether autonomous trucks would follow onto job sites, Voorhoeve said Volvo does not speculate on that.
“First of all, our main focus is now to continue in the vocational segment and to strengthen our position with a range that has far more applications available,” he said.

Logistics warehouse operator Prologis beat third-quarter expectations Thursday before the market opened, significantly raising its outlook for new developments.
Prologis ( NYSE: PLD ) reported consolidated revenue of $2.39 billion for the quarter, reflecting an 8% year-over-year increase and topping consensus estimates by 8%. Core funds from operations (FFO) of $1.60 per share were 11 cents higher y/y and 3 cents better than analysts’ expectations.
Lease signings in the period totaled 60 million square feet of space for the San Francisco-based real estate investment trust. Leases commenced totaled 55.9 million square feet, a 15% y/y decline.
Average occupancy improved 30 basis points y/y to 95.1%, 10 bps higher than the in second quarter . Net effective rent change on Prologis’ portfolio of multiyear leases was 38%, near the company’s full-year goal of 40%.
“Customers are running lean on inventory, and excess capacity within their networks has largely cleared,” said CEO Dan Letter. “We see healthy demand supported by e-commerce, advanced manufacturing and the build-out of the data center supply chain.”
Table: Prologis’ key performance indicators
The outlook for full-year 2026 core FFO was narrowed to a range of $6.25 to $6.29 per share, a 1-cent increase at the midpoint. The guide assumes average occupancy of 95.25% to 95.5% (25 bps lower at the high end of the range) and development starts between $5 billion and $5.75 billion (an 8% increase at the midpoint). The company previously raised its outlook for development starts by $1 billion in conjunction with its second-quarter report.
“Our financial results reflect another quarter of strong operating performance and disciplined capital allocation,” said Chief Financial Officer Tim Arndt. “That performance, together with the strength of our balance sheet, gives us the capacity and flexibility to continue investing in growth even in a higher interest rate environment.”
That growth plan includes the addition of London-based logistics warehouse operator Segro ( LSE.SGRO ).
Segro’s board agreed to Prologis’ $18.8-billion, best-and-final offer in July. The combination will expand Prologis’ European footprint by 47% to 368 million square feet. The combined entity will have $269 billion of assets under management.
“On SEGRO, shareholder approval was an important milestone in bringing our two companies together,” Letter said. “We look forward to completing the transaction and expanding our platform in Europe, increasing the scale at which we can serve customers.”
Shares of PLD were up 1.3% in early trading on Thursday compared to the S&P 500, which was down 0.5%
Prologis will host a call at noon EDT on Thursday to discuss third-quarter results.
Why it matters? Prologis’ third-quarter performance and development starts forecast reflect normalized inventory levels and robust demand from the e-commerce, advanced manufacturing and data center sectors. The company’s Segro acquisition will significantly expand its global footprint and infrastructure capacity to better serve international supply chains.

By Alex Lennane
15 October 2026
Former Apple and UPS executive Gal Dayan has just joined Ascent as COO, and talks big forwarders, tech – and aircraft ownership
Large freight forwarders are struggling to deliver the customer service their marketing promises, according to Mr Dayan, who argues that specialist operators have more room to invest in shipper relationships.
Mr Dayan, who became chief operating officer of Ascent Global Logistics on 1 October, told The Loadstar consolidation and the pursuit of efficiency had come at a cost to customers.
“I don’t feel that the multinationals truly value their customers,” he said.
Drawing on his experience as head of logistics at Apple, he questioned whether large forwarders’ claims to put customers ‘at the centre of their operations’ were reflected in the service they actually delivered.
“It’s been very challenging to really see the value the multinationals are bringing,” he said.
Mr Dayan, who also spent 23 years at UPS as SVP procurement, subsequently moved into marine and project logistics with Horizon Air Freight and Swift Marine, before joining Ascent.
He argued that the higher margins available in specialist logistics allowed providers to devote more resources to customers, while competing for general cargo required a different calculation.
“Can you go and serve all the verticals? Absolutely, you can,” he said, adding that the question was whether the return justified the investment.
Ascent has also focused on investment in technology to reduce the manual work involved in receiving orders, sourcing capacity, and preparing quotations, freeing staff to spend more time developing customer solutions.
The company is upgrading its proprietary PEAK marketplace, which connects customers with providers of services including expedited trucking, air charters, and onboard couriers. Separately, legacy transportation management systems in its brokerage operations are being replaced with a newer version of Oracle’s TM.
Gal Dayan
Mr Dayan said PEAK could return a proposed solution and quotation within six minutes of an enquiry. He contrasted this with the manual effort involved in arranging large numbers of charters ahead of Apple product launches.
But Ascent’s platform ambitions extend beyond its established automotive customer base, added.
“We have aspirations to actually continue to expand it, not just for the automotive, but to create a global platform that connects all the multinational airlines in the world with the freight forwarders and customers,” he said.
However, he did not give a launch timetable or explain how the proposed expansion would differ from existing airfreight booking platforms.
One of the most interesting aspects of Ascent is the fact that it owns aircraft via its USA Jet airline subsidiary, a notoriously difficult asset to manage, and one that has proved challenging for forwarders before. USA Jet has one MD-83F, and five MD-88Fs, while a further two are parked, according to planespotters.
The fleet has an average age of more than 35 years, and while cheap to own, they are not fuel efficient – 2013 data shows that on a trip between Miami and Memphis, an MD-88F would burn 13% more fuel than a 737-400F.
Mr Dayan acknowledged that the age of some aircraft was making spare parts harder to obtain. The airline was examining options for its next generation of aircraft, although he did not identify potential types or a replacement schedule.
Investment would be linked to demand and partnerships, he said, rather than fleet expansion for its own sake.
The airline remained central to Ascent’s proposition because it gave time-critical customers confidence that capacity would be available. The freighters operate on an adhoc charter basis through North America, Ascent’s main playground.
USA Jet remains “a critical element of our business”, confirmed Mr Dayan, although Ascent also uses partner airlines for longer-haul charters.
“We’re working now on a project from Korea, so we do offer our international charter services outside North America, relying on some other partners and not our fleet.”
On fleet investment, he added: “We don’t go and invest in new fleet just for the purpose of doing it,” explaining that expansion involved working with customers and strategic partners to ensure demand.
Mr Dayan sees further opportunities in life sciences and high-value technology shipments, where service requirements can outweigh relatively small differences in freight costs.
The hi-tech sector could be particularly interested in Ascent’s time-critical services for high-value shipments, combining shipment visibility and operational support with additional security.
“If we can package it with the proper security protocol, it will be a perfect answer for some of the high-value products that we’re able to provide to our customers,” he said.
But, he added: “I’m not suggesting that Apple is going to be my customer tomorrow, even though I have a great relationship with them. But I definitely see how the product we’re developing here will be very interesting to this hi-tech industry.”

Fall 2026 is really starting to feel like a turning point for the 2027 RV-ing season, what with the surprises in store from established manufacturers and new companies, new models, new construction methods, and new design ideas. This brand new fifth wheel RV would fall in that last category.
This is the 2027 Salem Hemisphere 383WDRK, which will also be sold under the Wildwood Heritage Glen 383WDRK name with differences only in terms of exterior and interior badging. It's a brand new floorplan in the Salem Hemisphere/Heritage Glen series, with a layout that's not necessarily new but it's interpreted in a way that you won't find anywhere else.
Both the Salem and the Wildwood brands operate under the Forest River umbrella, so this new floorplan was on display at the recent Dealer Expo, as a prototype. Content creator Ray from All About RVs says that he was personally involved in its development and that some things are bound to change inside before it goes into production, which is standard fare in the industry.
His video tour offers a much better appreciation of what makes this unit different from all the rest , better than the one posted by Forest River Direct, which you will also find at the bottom of the page.
Photo: Forest River The 383WDRK is a four-slide fifth wheel with a washer-dryer and a rear kitchen layout. Ray says that it's actually based on a popular but more expensive model from a different company, and that this is Forest River's more budget-friendly interpretation of it. That said, don't take budget-friendly to mean cheap or compromising: this RV is as nice as they get, with high quality finishes and a lot of focus on comfort and style.
As the headline says, the 383WDRK does everything differently, from the way it uses slide-outs to expand the available footprint to how it tries to think outside the box in the design of RV staples like a freestanding dinette or a half-bath. The result is a fifth wheel that oozes style and a surprising amount of functionality.
Coming in at 43 feet 9 inches (13.3 meters) of total length, the 383WDRK rides on a tandem axle and, as already noted, has four slide-outs in total, all of them flush within the floor and offered with marine-type woven carpeting. Not much is known about construction , except from what Ray says about the sidewalls being aluminum studded, foam block insulated, and with a layer of fiberglass painted in two tones of gray on the outside.
Photo: Forest River Direct You can see that the underbelly is fully enclosed and presumably heated, and all holding tanks have 12V heating pads on them. That means that this is a four-season RV, so it's perfect for extended vacations or even full-time living.
At the first look, the layout is typical for a fifth wheel: a front bedroom with a ensuite bathroom and a walk-in wardrobe in that front cap, and a rear kitchen that spills into the mid living room. The execution, though, is different from everything else.
For instance, the cooking block in the kitchen is in a smaller slide-out, so that it's recessed from the actual kitchen space, which feels larger because of this. The super-slide on the campsite side holds a massive dual-door stainless steel fridge with freezer, a pantry with sensor lights and plenty of space, and a dedicated coffee station. Nearby is a legless dining table mounted on the wall horizontally, so you can choose which view you want to look out on: the TV in the living room or the view out on the campsite.
Photo: Forest River Direct The living room is shown in the prototype with a loveseat/pull-out sofa in another small slide and a pair of theater seats with recliner function, right in front of the entertainment wall with the TV and the fireplace. This won't be the final design, though, because the theater seats are too bulky and take up too much space when the slides are closed, so the whole arrangement will probably be replaced by an L-shaped sectional sofa.
In front of the entrance is the "WD" part in the 838WDRK name, the washer-dryer laundry station. It's located in a half bath that's surprisingly elegant and spacious, with a round stainless steel sink and open storage, a porcelain toilet, and a stacked washer and dryer under more cabinets. This isn't a full-on laundry station, but it's the closest thing.
The main bedroom is on the upper deck, with a king bed with a large storage compartment underneath, a dresser with an integrated vanity table that all women will simply love , and prep for a second TV. From here, you move into the ensuite bathroom – a generously sized space with dual vanities, solid surface counters, an oversize mirror, a porcelain toilet, a linen closet, and a large one-piece fiberglass shower with glass doors and a skylight.
Photo: Forest River Direct The full wardrobe is at the very front, and again, it's bound to be a ladies' favorite. Featuring a wraparound hanging rod, another dresser with drawers, a bench, and deep cubbies for shoe storage, it's a walk-in space where fashion will feel right at home. Sorry not sorry.
Storage outside includes a front compartment for the batteries and the spare wheel, a cavernous pass-through with several points of access, and a nice storage solution for fishing rods.
Standard features will include an 18,000-BTU Furrion Chill Cube AC in the living room, a ducted 15,000-BTU one in the bedroom, an on-demand water heater, a furnace, GE residential appliances, and two power awnings with LED lights. Also standard is 6-point electric auto-leveling, a 200W solar panel on the roof, full-length barreled ceilings, and square windows with built-in shades and thermafoil reflective backing.
Photo: Forest River Direct Most specs are still listed as TBD ("to be determined") as of this writing, but dry weight will be at around 14,300 lbs (6.486 kg). Retail price is almost $125,000, with Ray mentioning a minimum advertised pricing of $77,499.
Forest River and the entire team are still taking feedback on this floorplan, so there's no word yet on when it might arrive at dealerships.

By Gavin van Marle
15 October 2026
UK lobbyists today pushed back at attempts to have the EU designate the ports of Felixstowe, London, and Southampton as “neighbouring container transhipment ports”, in the ongoing question of whether shippers are rerouting cargo to avoid ETS scheme charges.
In July, the EU ETS Observatory – developed by Spain’s state-owned ports administrator Puertos del Estado as a way of monitoring “carbon leakage” from its transhipment hub of Algeciras to Morocco’s Tanger Med after the introduction of EU-ETS at the beginning of 2024 – published a report which appeared to suggest that the container volume growth seen in UK ports during 2025 was the direct result of shippers seeking to minimise EU-ETS charges.
It had led to a “reduction in the connectivity of container traffic for long-distance services operated at EU ports, compared with neighbouring countries not subject to European environmental regulations, measured in terms of the teu-mile parameter”.
London Gateway owner DP World said its 2025 throughput at the port was just over 3m teu, a rise of 52% on 2024, while Felixstowe’s throughput was 3.6m teu, flat year on year. UK Department for Transport data shows UK-wide container volumes up by 600,0000 teu.
However, the British Ports Association (BPA) today argued that 2025’s volume growth seen at the UK’s three main ports was caused by a combination of new capacity coming onstream at London Gateway and the reorganisation of the deepsea shipping alliances that took place at the start of the year.
One the chief effects of the new alliance networks was the switch of Maersk from Felixstowe to London Gateway, as the Gemini Cooperation’s chief Asia-Europe UK port.
“Of the approximately 600,000 additional container units handled nationally, London accounted for around 500,000. The DfT explicitly links London’s increase to additional capacity at London Gateway. This is not the pattern that would most naturally be expected from a general UK wide regulatory advantage.
“The overwhelming majority of national growth occurred in the port area where a major new tranche of container capacity had just become available,” the BPA paper stated.
It also argued that measuring traffic by teu-miles was not a “measure of the containers handled by a port, the cargo imported or exported through it, vessel utilisation or conventional cargo market share”.
“The metric is particularly sensitive to port-call sequencing,” it added. “Consider an Asia-North Europe service that calls at both Rotterdam and Felixstowe; if Rotterdam is the first European call, the long intercontinental leg is associated with Rotterdam.
“Reverse those two calls and the UK’s measured transport work can rise sharply, even if the same vessel continues to call at both ports and the amount of cargo handled at each changes little.”
However, as The Loadstar reported in September, recent analysis by freight intelligence platform VesselBot shows EU importers with cargo on an Asia-Europe vessel which calls at the UK before continental Europe, have been faced with significantly lower ETS charges than if an EU port was its first call.
However, the BPA also notes that, with the UK also set to introduce a carbon charging mechanism designed to largely align with the EU, the cost differential is expected to exist for a relatively short window.
“The current UK–EU carbon-pricing difference is itself transitional: the UK ETS Authority has proposed extending the scheme to 50% of emissions from international voyages from 2028, mirroring the present EU approach.
“EU ETS may affect the economics of some individual rotations at the margin. But the structural explanation for the UK’s stronger position lies in long-planned investment, increased capacity, carrier-network restructuring, and operational performance.
“UK connectivity gains should therefore not be characterised as regulatory avoidance or carbon leakage, without much stronger evidence that the activity concerned would otherwise have taken place at EU ports,” it says.
