Chevrolet Camaro ZL1s are cool, but few are cooler than this example, which boasts numerous mods, has more power to play with, and is for sale in the United States of America.
Modded by Hendrick Motorsports and Callaway, it is called the Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 Coupe Hertz/Hendrick Motorsports Edition (Jeez, that’s a long name!), and you are looking at car #7 out of 24 built to this specification, as per the dashboard plaque. The muscle car in question is a 2020 model year, with 14,300 miles (23,000 km) under its belt, a clean California title, and a clean Carfax vehicle history report, meaning that it hasn’t been involved in any accidents, and has no mileage discrepancies.
The equipment list is extensive and comprises stuff such as the TripleCooled intercooler system and GenThree supercharger from Callaway, a set of 20-inch wheels finished in black with custom center caps, Hertz fender badges, Hertz yellow-finished brake calipers with the Hendrick Motorsports logo on them, a special build plaque with the VIN located under the hood, and oil filler cap, coolant reservoir cap, and brake reservoir cap with the #24 logo. The Hendrick Motorsports dashboard plaque with a signature and production number is also on deck.
Additional goodies of this 2020 Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 Coupe Hertz/Hendrick Motorsports Edition include the Recaro Performance bucket seats for the driver and front passenger complete with embroidered headrests, embroidered floor and trunk mats, Hertz yellow-painted trim on the door cards, illuminated door sills that feature the Hertz logo on them, and a few other things. The listing also reveals the OEM hood insert with a cutout for the supercharger, a 1LE spoiler, and Diode Dynamics smoked side markers.
Photo: Cars&Bids As for the equipment installed at the factory during the muscle car’s production, it includes the head-up display, rear park assist, Magnetic Ride Control suspension, Brembo brakes, and limited-slip differential. Any muscle car enthusiast and their grandmother can tell you that this generation Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 came with a 6.2-liter supercharged V8, which pumped out 650 hp (485 kW/659 ps) and 650 pound-feet (881 Nm) of torque with no modifications whatsoever.
The stock vehicle required in the region of three and a half seconds to hit 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill, and took a little over 11 seconds to run the standing quarter mile. However, due to some of the mods, this Chevy Camaro ZL1 is punchier. The engine is said to produce 750 hp (559 kW/760 ps) and 739 lb-ft (1,002 Nm) of torque, and it drives the rear wheels through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The performance hasn’t been mentioned in the ad, but we know that this model needed 3.2 seconds to hit the 60 mph mark.
Other than some chips on the front-facing surfaces, there are no other known issues, as this 2020 Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 Coupe Hertz/Hendrick Motorsports Edition is in top-notch condition. The vehicle’s recent service history reveals that it had a four-wheel alignment performed in January 2023, September 2022, January 2022, and October 2022, at 7,145, 6815, 6,350, and 6,244 miles (11,499, 10,968, 10,219, 10,049 km), respectively. The engine oil and filter were changed in December and January 2024.
Photo: Cars&Bids Besides the muscle car, the next owner will get some service records, the owner’s manual, window sticker, a Hertz/Hendrick Motorsports build sheet, a Callaway Certificate of Authenticity and wall plaque, the Callaway carbon fiber engine cover signed by Reeves Callaway, a spare carbon fiber hood scoop, the OEM spoiler and sidemarkers, and one key.
The seller reportedly bought this modified and rare Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 in early 2023, adding some 6,600 miles (10,600 km) since, and he hasn’t revealed why he wants it gone. Interested parties should know that the title will only be available after the loan has been paid off, as there is a loan on this machine, and the sale proceeds will be used to satisfy it.
Given that the 2020 Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 Coupe Hertz/Hendrick Motorsports Edition is a rare model, it is tricky to find out how much it is worth in today’s used car market in the United States of America. However, it appears that on average, this thing sells for approximately $90,000, and that’s more than the regular ZL1 version of the Chevy Camaro from the same model year, which fetches from $50,000 to over $80,000, depending on the usual factors.
As you can imagine, there is a reserve on it, and at $35,000, which was the highest bid at the time of writing, it obviously hasn’t been met. This modded ZL1 is going under the gavel as we speak on Cars&Bids, and the ongoing online auction will end on October 21, 2026. You can bid on it here , and before you click that link, feel free to tell us how much this machine is worth to you.

Following several recent initiatives, the FDA’s newest rare disease framework sets out to standardize the agency’s approach to scientific evidence and bring rare disease therapies to patients faster.
The FDA revealed a new framework Wednesday for its approach to rare disease drug regulation built to encourage innovation by standardizing the way clinical trial requirements are applied across diseases.
To allow for a faster and more systematic path for as many as 10,000 different rare conditions affecting 30 million Americans, the FDA said drug development should account for nuance by approaching each disease based on the evidence that can be realistically generated in small patient populations.
“As we learn more about rare diseases and better understand the breadth of suffering they cause, we must ensure that America’s regulatory system remains at the forefront—prepared to respond to emerging science, anticipate the needs of patients and families, and help bring safe and effective therapies to those who need them,” Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said in a prepared statement accompanying the announcement of the Rare Disease Framework Initiative.
In a white paper elaborating on the new framework, the agency touted its current rare disease programs, including the FDA Rare Disease Innovation Hub , the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)’s Accelerating Rare disease Cures (ARC) program and the Rare Disease Endpoint Advancement (RDEA) pilot program , a collaboration between CDER and the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER).
“We need to build on, systematize and operationalize these individual efforts into a consistently utilized, cross-center approach that champions the use of cutting-edge science, novel methodologies and innovative statistical approaches,” the FDA wrote.
Just 5% of rare diseases currently have an FDA-approved treatment, according to the agency’s announcement. The agency is committed to “providing greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in regulatory decision-making,” incorporating the patient’s voice, bringing in external experts and shared resources and applying risk-based approaches—especially in chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review and pre-approval inspections.
The Rare Disease Framework Initiative follows the “ plausible mechanism ” pathway introduced in November 2025 by former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary to expedite treatments for diseases with exceedingly small patient populations, for which a randomized trial would not be feasible.

“What makes this initiative especially important is the opportunity to move beyond case-by-case regulatory accommodations toward a framework designed around the scientific realities of rare diseases,” Gavin added.
The Alliance for Regenerative Medicine (ARM) also commended the FDA’s effort to set rare diseases apart, giving them the individual attention they need as opposed to rubber-stamping an ill-fitting regulatory method.
“The agency rightly recognizes that a regulatory system built for common diseases cannot simply be repurposed for rare disorders,” ARM wrote in a statement, noting that the framework’s success in the cell and gene therapy space will depend on forthcoming FDA guidance and rulemaking with regard to allowing single-arm trials and natural history data.
Indeed, many of the FDA’s highest-profile recent reversals of guidance have centered around the use of external controls. In November last year, the agency disagreed with previous FDA guidance allowing uniQure’s Phase 1/2 study—which used a natural history external control—to support a regulatory application for its Huntington’s disease gene therapy AMT-130. And the use of an externally controlled study was “one of the major issues” raised in the July 2025 complete response letter for Capricor’s deramiocel, being developed for Duchenne muscular dystrophy cardiomyopathy, CEO Linda Marbán said during a BioSpace webinar in March.
The FDA has set an Oct. 28 meeting to discuss the framework, soliciting feedback from patients, advocates and members of the industry.

© Ian Wilson
By Charlotte Goldstone
15 October 2026
LATAM Cargo has reported a 150% increase in pharmaceutical air cargo shipments between Europe and Brazil in the first seven months of the year, driven largely by rising demand for GLP-1-based medications.
The growth, on the same period in 2025, comes after the carrier transported nearly 32,000 tonnes of cargo between the two markets, an increase of 27% year on year.
GLP-1 medicines, used in treatments for type 2 diabetes, accounted for approximately 15% of LATAM Cargo’s total Europe-Brazil volume during the period.
Jorge Carretero, cargo sales manager Europe at LATAM Airlines Group, said: “The growth in pharmaceutical transport demonstrates how demand for specialised logistics solutions is gaining prominence between Europe and Brazil. Our priority is to support this evolution through a safe, efficient operation equipped for the specific requirements of each cargo type.
“At the same time, the 27% growth in volume reinforces the importance of connectivity between both markets and our network’s capacity to serve diverse economic sectors.”
However, the increase on the Europe-Brazil corridor contrasts with a more subdued picture across the wider pharmaceutical air freight market.
Maarten Wormer, head of consulting at Aevean, told The Loadstar, at Aviation Connect in Athens this month, that pharma air freight volumes had been broadly flat in the first part of the year, with some changes in trade flows rather than widespread growth.
He noted that some GLP-1 shipments originating in Denmark were being moved away from air freight, potentially reflecting greater competition and the availability of alternative transport modes as supplies expanded beyond their initial markets.
“It’s not just coming from Denmark anymore, so it can now go via ocean, because the first waves of the goods have gone out,” he explained, and added that there could be multiple reasons for the modal shift.
Growth in pharmaceutical logistics was increasingly concentrated in high-value products, including cell and gene therapies, requiring more intensive monitoring throughout transport, he said.
For LATAM Cargo, Germany, Belgium, Spain, and Italy were the leading European origins for pharmaceutical shipments to Brazil between January and July, followed by the Netherlands and France. Services included belly capacity on routes such as Lisbon-São Paulo and Madrid-São Paulo, as well as freighter connections from Frankfurt and Brussels to Viracopos.
The carrier said its pharmaceutical handling measures included temperature monitoring, climate-controlled rooms, cargo segregation, thermal blankets, and reduced ramp exposure. Active temperature-controlled containers can be connected to power, with batteries and temperatures monitored periodically.
The importance of qualified routes was also highlighted during an industry panel discussion at the EU CBEC Cross Border Ecommerce Forum in Liege last month. Julia Celetaria, a global pharma director and healthcare specialist, cautioned that adding a route did not automatically create a suitable alternative for pharmaceutical cargo.
“Is it an alternative? No, it’s not for pharma,” she said, emphasising the need for qualified airports and routes, trained personnel, and appropriate standard operating procedures.
Meanwhile, DHL Global Forwarding has expanded its Health Logistics Cold Chain Network with six dedicated air corridors linking Europe and North America with markets in Asia. The new connections include routes from Liège and Brussels to Shanghai, Brussels to Singapore, and Cincinnati to Singapore, Tokyo Narita, and Seoul Incheon.
It said the expansion reflected continued investment in dedicated healthcare logistics capacity.

2023 Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 Fights Off Depreciation Like Rocky Balboa, Sells for Little Below MSRP
29 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
Depreciation is an unavoidable part of car ownership, whether it's a high-performance model or your run-of-the-mill family crossover. There are, of course, exceptions, and tons of them. The Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 stands out when it comes to value retention, especially among other muscle cars. Be honest, wouldn't you rather have a ZL1 than pretty much anything else? I'm asking all you driving enthusiasts out there, as opposed to drag racing aficionados.
As fate would have it, not all flagship Camaros are created equal, as a result of GM offering the optional 1LE Extreme Track Performance Package. It's responsible for the Performance suspension with Multimatic DSSV dampers, but also the front dive planes, a dual-mode exhaust system, 19" forged wheels, plus a carbon-fiber hood insert and rear wing.
The result is one of the most track-capable muscle cars ever produced, and when you add the fact that GM discontinued Camaro production in late 2023 with no official successor announced, well, you can understand why used ZL1s are still fetching close to their original MSRP at auction.
Let's take this 2023 model year example, wearing Black like the "dark knight" that it is. Visually, it also comes with a Satin Black hood, all the carbon fiber bits you get with the 1LE Extreme Track Performance Package, and clear taillight lenses. The black-finished 19" split five-spoke forged wheels are wearing Goodyear Eagle F1 Supercar 3R rubber, while stopping power is provided by the ventilated Brembo discs with the red-finished calipers.
The original MSRP for this beauty was $80,460. And now, a dealer out of Scottsdale, Arizona, just sold the car for $75,000 (plus a buyer's fee) with only 2,300 miles on the clock. I'd call this a good deal for both parties - but especially the buyer. Sure, you can get a cheaper ZL1 than this, but not by much, and perhaps not with this exact spec.
Meanwhile, interior highlights include the heated and ventilated Recaro front seats trimmed in Jet Black leather and sueded microfiber, a Bose sound system, a head-up display, keyless entry, automatic climate control, cruise control, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity, a heated microsuede-wrapped steering wheel, and more.
Photo: Bring a Trailer As for performance, we're dealing with a supercharged 6.2-liter LT4 V8 , pushing a factory rating of 650 horsepower and 650 lb-ft of torque. Everything gets sent to the rear wheels via a 10-speed automatic transmission and an electronic limited-slip differential.
In a straight line, the ZL1 can accelerate to 60 mph (97 kph) in about 3.5 seconds. This 10-speed auto version is about 0.2 seconds quicker off the mark than the 6-speed manual variant. Although, I think a lot of collectors would actually prefer the latter. Some enthusiasts too.

Renault Built Its Most Expensive Car Ever and Already Got Over 1,000 Orders for It
13 photos
Photo: Renault
Renault has officially secured over 1,100 orders for the Renault 5 Turbo 3E. Despite the jaw-dropping price, which makes it the most expensive production Renault ever, demand for the all-electric drift missile has been exceptionally strong since the moment reservations opened.
The first batch of 700 allocations, comprising 500 customer spots and 200 dealer network spots, sold out in a matter of hours. Renault brand CEO Fabrice Cambolive confirmed that more than half of the total production run of 1,980 units is already spoken for.
Buyers from Europe, Japan, the Middle East, and Australia have placed deposits to lock in their build slots. Renault estimates that the remaining allocations will sell out before customer deliveries officially begin in early 2028.
The Renault 5 Turbo 3E is the most expensive production car ever built by the French automaker. It completely shatters any record, with a staggering starting price of 155,000 euros, which is the equivalent of roughly $173,700 for the first 500 units. Following the initial launch window, the official base price transitions to 160,000 euros ($179,311).
Photo: Renault Prior to the arrival of the 5 Turbo 3E, the most expensive production Renault was the track-focused Megane RS Trophy-R , which started at around 96,000 euros ($107,660). However, due to the extensive customization possibilities, Renault Group CEO Francois Provost noted that heavily personalized builds are expected to climb to over 350,000 euros ($392,500).
But to get there, prospective buyers must first complete a dedicated priority interest form through the official Renault platform. Once the enquiry is approved, Renault matches the buyer with a local dealership to arrange a formal, in-person consultation. To officially secure a build slot, customers must first secure a build slot by wiring a 50,000-euro deposit, which will be fully credited toward the final balance, set to be invoiced upon configuration.
Because only 1,980 vehicles will see the light of day, early customers are granted a priority perk: they will have the option to pay a premium to pick their car’s chassis production number, a move that is subject to availability.
The customization program won't start before mid-2027. Future owners will work directly with Renault designers. The option list includes extreme retro-neon racing liveries, classic heritage color schemes, like the iconic 1980s Rouge Grenade or the 1982 Tour de Corse yellow-and-black rally look. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in early 2028.
Photo: Renault Florent Ingargiola, the car's product leader confirmed the over 1,000 orders in a conversation with Piston Heads.
What are customers getting for the money? The Renault-badged pocket rocket is powered by a dual-motor powertrain, with both motors mounted in the back, powering each rear wheel independently. The setup produces 547 horsepower (555 metric horsepower) and 516 pound-feet (700 Newton meters) of torque.
It can flash from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph) in 3.5 seconds, hit 124 mph (200 kph) in 9.0 seconds, and max out at 167 mph (270 kph). The car is sitting on an 800-volt architecture and is equipped with a 70-kWh battery pack, which can store enough energy for a drive of up to 248 miles (400 kilometers) before it needs to be plugged in again.
The Renault 5 Turbo 3E measures 160.6 inches (4,080 millimeters) in length, 79.9 inches (2,030 millimeters) in width, and 54.3 inches (1,380 millimeters) in height, sitting on a wheelbase of 101.2 inches (2,570 millimeters).
With that sort of price and that sort of oomph, the 5 Turbo 3E is in a league of ts own with no rival in the market today or any time soon.

By Daniil Davydoff Following the U.S. parcel delivery market can feel like tracking a race. Tactical moves to increase network capacity, build facilities, and launch tools, as well as strategic changes in leadership and operating models, dominate assessments of which carriers are gaining or losing ground, but political and policy forces are shaping those decisions.
Labor dynamics, global instability, and supply chain resilience and security may ultimately determine which carrier is the winning “tortoise” or the losing “hare” more than commercial and operational considerations.
New labor dynamics are putting pressure on several models. Teamster negotiations are hitting unionized carriers, while fast-growing “alternative carriers” using gig-based delivery models are facing increased scrutiny over compliance with labor protections. That scrutiny is increasingly playing out in court, through lawsuits alleging violations of state labor codes and the Fair Labor Standards Act.
Last month, DoorDash and Uber reached a $131.5 million settlement with New York City’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. Some alternative carriers and large shipping platforms, including Amazon, have sought to shield themselves from the true cost of carrying fulltime employees by using delivery service providers, but that may not be an option in the future.
New York City’s Delivery Protection Act, supported by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, would require companies to hire core warehouse and delivery workers directly rather than rely on DSPs. Chicago’s version would add licensing, training, and safety requirements.
The result is that no parcel labor model looks politically uncomplicated anymore. Whether you rely on unionized networks, gig platforms, or DSP-based operations, there are new questions about who bears the cost, risk, and responsibility of last-mile delivery and associated operations.
Geopolitics complicate parcel delivery
Links between global politics and domestic parcel delivery are not always obvious at first, but in 2026 the impact of conflict and trade policy is becoming harder to miss.
The Iran war has pushed fuel prices higher, and those elevated costs are expected to persist. FarEye recently reported that 88% of operators say delivery costs are growing as fast as revenue, or faster, with fuel among the top three cost pressures. For shippers, the war has translated into higher fuel surcharges. According to analysis by AFS Logistics , fuel surcharges that were about 9% for UPS and FedEx in 2021 are now above 23% for both carriers.
If cost remains a primary driver of carrier selection then geopolitics is no longer an abstraction. It is becoming a material input into shipper decisions.
Trade policy is creating a similar shift. The permissive de minimis environment helped discount cross-border marketplaces and sellers thrive and supported alternative carriers positioned to serve them. With de minimis now removed, those foreign e-commerce giants face a tougher U.S. outlook even as they make costly investments in local fulfillment to adapt. The political risk may not end there, as suggested by the ongoing FTC investigation into cross-border retailer Shein. For the emerging carriers that grew alongside these platforms and sellers, geopolitics is now taking back some of what it initially gave, pushing them into a more crowded and difficult search for domestic customers.
Political anxiety over dependence on foreign trade is also turning inward, with parcel-market integrity increasingly framed as a U.S. economic security issue. That policy focus is still in an early stage, but the clearest example is Sen. Tom Cotton’s call for the Department of Justice to investigate alternative carriers he argues unfairly threaten U.S. firms, jobs, and data.
Importance of risk management infrastructure
Scrutiny is likely to intensify on the data and compliance front. Less than a week after Cotton’s letter was published, news broke that SpeedX, one of the companies mentioned in it, exposed 840 million customer records in one of the largest delivery-industry data incidents to date . Since then, other incidents have underscored the fragility of delivery networks, including a cyberattack on Boston Scientific, which disrupted its ability to process and ship customer orders and will likely affect its ability to meet some of its targets for the year.
A future reckoning with automation and AI in parcel delivery could push technology regulation and data security compliance even further up the agenda. Several forms of AI — particularly AI analytics and agentic AI — are expected to have high impact on the logistics industry, and many carriers are already investing in AI-enabled technologies, including autonomous applications.
There have not yet been major, well-publicized logistics failures tied directly to AI systems. But as general-purpose models have shown a tendency to fabricate information or behave unpredictably, it is not difficult to imagine similar concerns emerging in parcel operations, where algorithmic decisions increasingly affect routing, fraud detection, customer service, warehouse activity, and delivery orchestration. In that environment, AI will not be treated merely as an efficiency tool; it may become another test of whether parcel networks can be trusted.
Political and policy dynamics do not negate the importance of strategy, cost, reliability, and speed in determining carrier success, but they imply that the next phase of parcel competition may reward a broader set of strengths. As shippers diversify their carrier portfolios, the most durable partnerships will likely depend not only on price or service levels, but also on continuity, regulatory discipline, labor stability, data security, and predictable performance in a less predictable environment.
For carriers, the tech-sector philosophy of “move fast and break things” may no longer be enough. In a market where politics increasingly shapes the rules of the race, the most valuable networks may not always be the fastest movers or the loudest disruptors. They may be the ones built to keep moving when the track changes.
( Daniil Davydoff is senior manager, market intelligence and strategy at DHL eCommerce Americas. His views do not reflect those of his company or FreightWaves. He can be contacted on LinkedIn or at daniil.davydoff@dhl.com .)

WASHINGTON — As the deadline approaches for defense industry to ween themselves off critical minerals from adversary nations, the Army is expecting to see “some impact” on companies that are still struggling to comply, an Army official said.
Executive order (EO) 14415, which was released in July, gives a January 2027 deadline for US companies to stop using critical materials and minerals from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. Companies will be able to get a waiver only if the government approves their mitigation plan, which spells out concrete steps that the firm is taking to find new suppliers in the United States or partner nations.
Liz Miranda, Army Materiel Command’s executive deputy to the commanding general, said Wednesday the EO’s requirements for companies to map their supply chain down to the raw material level “is no easy task.”
“We’re working towards that. Are we there yet? No. So we are going to see some impact come January,” she told an audience at the Association for the US Army conference.
Asked by Breaking Defense what impacts the Army foresees, Miranda said that she doesn’t anticipate any “off the cliff” outcomes that would be catastrophic for the service.
Rather, she said, “ I see a gradual holding all of us accountable to mitigating those areas where we know we we have risk because we’re dependent on foreign adversaries.”
Critical minerals covered by the EO include substances like tungsten alloys, which is used in engine components and hypersonics, and germanium, which is used in thermal imaging systems. China is the dominant producer of both materials, according to a September report by the Aerospace Industries Association (AIA).
Miranda pointed to the Army’s announcement earlier this week that it will conduct a “manufacturing rodeo,” which is meant to expose supply chain and manufacturing risks that the service may not be aware of.
“Unfortunately, we cannot insource all of the parts that are required — specifically for drone dominance,” she said. “So with this rodeo, what we intend to do is really look internal to the US domestic capabilities and see what gaps exist, and then working with industry to invest in building that domestic capability or partnering with other allies to identify resources there that we can leverage to scale what we need.”
In a July interview, Michael Cadenazzi, the assistant secretary of defense for industrial base policy, told Breaking Defense that the Pentagon would be willing to work with companies who need waivers, provided they are making a good faith effort to find new sources of supply.
“What we need to do is commit to companies to say, ‘Look, how are you going to go ahead and resolve this problem through friendshoring, through domestic shoring, through changes in suppliers?” he said. “And if there’s a gap, a legitimate gap, [and] you have a plan and you need a window to see you through [to] bridge that gap, that’s what we want to know.”
However, defense trade groups have raised concerns about the EO’s quick timeline. AIA has argued that waivers will still be necessary for years after the January 2027 deadline, as the current domestic supply of critical minerals is not sufficient to meet companies’ needs.
In the September report, AIA found, “Significant domestic processing, refining, and magnet production capacity for aerospace-grade materials is not expected to be available until 2028 or later,” with additional certification and qualification activities potentially pushing that date even further down the road.
The EO makes those challenges “more acute” because waivers will be restricted to companies who get a mitigation plan approved, with little feedback from the government on what constitutes an acceptable plan, said Dak Hardwick, AIA Vice President of International Affairs.
“Industry is still looking for clarity around the mitigation-plan standard and processing timelines,” he said Tuesday. “AIA is urging industry, government, Congress, and minerals producers to work together on a practical path forward that meets the unique needs of our industry, preserves waivers where qualified supply does not yet exist, and avoids disruptions to defense production.”

As Tesla Is Dragging Its Feet, Third Parties Prepare Native CarPlay and AirPlay Integration
8 photos
Photo: @mikegapinski via X
Michal Gapinski, who developed the Tesla Android Project to bring Apple CarPlay to Tesla EVs, announced a breakthrough. Its new project, CoilShift, will enable CarPlay natively, without needing a dongle or a browser. Besides CarPlay, CoilShift will also enable AirPlay, allowing users more flexibility with the content sent to their Tesla's display.
Much like the Roadster that will be demoed tonight, Apple CarPlay on Tesla EVs is a Schroedinger's cat of possibilities. Rumors that Tesla was working with Apple to implement CarPlay natively surfaced last year. However, nothing has changed since then, and the project might have been axed already. That's because the market conditions have changed significantly since then.
On the one hand, Tesla and Apple had a rollercoaster relationship, and 2025 CarPlay rumors surfaced when it was at its peak. Apple Car was scrapped, while sales of Tesla EVs were falling, so Musk did not see the partnership as a threat, but as an enabler. However, it's the other way around now, with Musk's SpaceX at odds with Apple over choosing Google Gemini as its AI provider. Tesla sales are booming , so there's no incentive to change direction.
Besides that, Tesla has plugged some of the holes that made owners wish to have CarPlay support. Grok Assistant can now perform many tasks in a Tesla, including replying to texts and emails. The only thing of value that Apple CarPlay support could bring to the table is better navigation and route planning in countries where Tesla Nav sucks. This includes Eastern Europe, and it's not surprising that the first and best third-party CarPlay provider was born there.
I'm talking about Tesla Android Project, developed by Polish developer Michal Gapinski. This came the closest to a native experience, even though a Raspberry Pi device was required to relay internet traffic. The setup allowed Gapinski to run CarPlay in the Tesla Browser. Other third-party accessory providers tried the same route to offer Apple CarPlay support in Tesla EVs.
However, Gapinski has worked on a better solution. He and Maciej Wilczynski founded CoilShift with the aim of bringing new features to Tesla EVs, including CarPlay. Instead of using a dongle and the Tesla Browser, CoilShift does that natively, through its own app. It's unclear at this stage whether Tesla will support it. CoilShift uses a known exploit in Tesla MCU3, which might be patched later. Tesla could also take more drastic measures to block CoilShift.
The good news is that CoilShift provides the same experience that Tesla partnering with Apple should've offered . The CarPlay interface sits in its own window, as Tesla might have intended it, without interfering with the rest of the UI. Everything works natively, including Siri commands through the car's microphone and lossless audio. The cherry on the cake is the RGB ambient light strip pulsing to the music.
CoilShift also enables AirPlay, allowing owners to project all sorts of content from their phones or laptops, including movies via streaming services. As Wilczynski noted, it's like having an external display for your Mac, iPhone, or iPad, built into your car's dashboard. So far, CoilShift is not ready for primetime, but that should change soon. Unless Tesla decides on this Schroedinger's cat, that is. I am in tears of joy. Microphone for Siri works, lossless audio works and you can hear it. 12/10. I don't care about maps, music alone makes it worth it. https://t.co/olDz9qjqpH — Michał Gapiński (@mikegapinski) October 13, 2026 CarPlay on a @CoilShift-enabled Tesla was presented to you by @mikegapinski yesterday. But that’s just one of the many, many things I’ve been cooking lately. Today I have the pleasure to share with you another useful feature that CoilShift unlocks: AirPlay! It’s like having an external display for your Mac, iPhone or iPad - but built into your car! This is just an early development preview - the finished version will not feature those ugly black borders and will be able to fill the entire car screen. Despite many rumours about Tesla planning to add official AirPlay support, I’ve found no existing plumbing for it anywhere in the firmware. Everything about this feature has been implemented from scratch. How cool is that? — Maciej P. Wilczyński (@maciej) October 14, 2026

Stargate Daedalus Set Is Proof Not Only Star Wars and Star Trek Ships Are Cool in LEGO Form
9 photos
Photo: LEGO Ideas/SamSamSamy
Ask any sci-fi lover out there which universe has the best spaceships, and the response will always include, high up on the list, Star Trek, Star Wars, and, to some extent, Battlestar Galactica. But there is one TV series that almost always gets overlooked, although, in my opinion, shouldn't.
That TV universe is called Stargate, and if you’ve only skimmed the surface of it instead of watching all 350+ episodes of the three main series, then you’re probably wondering what spaceships have to do with it. Well, let me explain.
At its core, Stargate does not need spaceships to send its main character to other planets – it simply uses a stargate to connect two locations in our galaxy through an Einstein–Rosen bridge. A wormhole, if you will.
For years on end, those responsible for the series have made the most of the Stargates spread across the galaxy by an ancient race, but as things got more and more complex, the need for spaceships became apparent. So the writers introduced them, first in the service of alien races that are up to no good, and then in the hands of the human race.
One of these human ships is the one called Daedalus, first mentioned in the main series, SG-1, but not shown on screen until the Atlantis spin-off came along. Made in-house by the Tau'ri (that’s how the alien races call humans), it was the second-generation capital ship used by the U.S. military.
Since its introduction in the second season of Atlantis , the Daedalus has played a pivotal role in defending the humans and aliens who relied on it, fighting off the Wraith, the Replicators, and the Hybrids.
For one reason or another, the toymaking world doesn’t seem to think that the Daedalus is worthy of being replicated in the real world, and that’s why we never got, for instance, a LEGO set dedicated to it.
That could (and should) change, thanks to the efforts of a LEGO Ideas fan creator who goes by the handle SamSamSamy. In August last year, this person submitted their idea on the Stargate Atlantis Daedalus, and the project has been fighting to get enough backers to keep going up the corporate ladder.
The designer has tried this idea before, so this set is basically a reworked and bettered one, with some modifications made to its exterior, more details, and extra hardware (like, say antennas) added.
Put together using 1,440 parts of plastic (quite a large number for an Ideas set), the completed Daedalus measures 24 x 10.1 x 8.2 inches (62 x 26 x 21 cm), making it impossible to miss when displayed somewhere.
At the time of writing, this LEGO Ideas project has 1,309 backers and 181 days left to get to 5,000. By the looks of it, it won’t make it, but one never knows. Especially now that a Stargate reboot is in the works from Prime Video.

Vanda Pharmaceuticals is suspending the development of a social anxiety drug licensed from Novartis after the drug showed no significant benefit in a late-stage study.
The investigational drug, called VQW-765, failed to significantly ease distress versus placebo in patients with social anxiety disorder during a social stress test, according to an announcement on Wednesday. The analysis focused on female participants, for whom the drug was previously found to be more effective.
“This was a clean miss, not a near miss,” Oppenheimer analysts told investors in a Wednesday note.
Vanda has decided to put the VQW-765 program on hold “pending further analysis of the full dataset,” the biotech said.
The Phase 3 study, called VP-VQW-765-3201 , enrolled 546 adults with social anxiety disorder deemed to have elevated anxiety levels at baseline, as measured by validated scales. After receiving either VQW-765 or placebo, participants were asked to go through a standardized social stress test that requires them to prepare and deliver a presentation to a panel. The study’s primary outcome was distress and nervousness during the stress test in female participants, assessed using a self-reported tool, according to Vanda’s release.
VQW-765 is a small-molecule partial agonist of the alpha 7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, the activation of which could help alleviate symptoms of anxiety and depression. Vanda picked up the drug candidate in a December 2014 settlement agreement with Novartis regarding certain disputes over the antipsychotic drug Fanapt. Alongside a $25 million equity investment, the pharma granted Vanda an exclusive worldwide license to VQW-765, which at the time was called AQW051.
Phase 2 data published in July 2025 showed that patients on VQW-765 experienced lower self-reported anxiety during a standard social stress test, though the drug’s effect in the overall study population fell short of statistical significance. Stratifying by sex, results showed that VQW-765 was more effective in females, in whom the anxiety-easing effect was significant; VQW-765’s benefits in males remained non-significant.
“We are disappointed that Study 3201 did not confirm the earlier Phase II findings for VQW-765 in patients with social anxiety disorder,” Vanda CEO Mihael Polymeropoulos said in a prepared statement on Wednesday.
Analysts at Oppenheimer do not expect the Phase 3 miss to be highly detrimental to Vanda. VQW-765 “sat only in our bull case, so there is no change to our estimates” for the biopharma, the firm said. Oppenheimer continues to rate the biotech at outperform, suggesting it expects Vanda to deliver high returns for investors.
Still, the VQW-765 pause is likely to add “pressure to the rest of the portfolio,” Oppenheimer said. Two of the three late-stage readouts the firm was keeping tabs on have already dropped, the analysts noted. The first came in September, when Hetlioz met the primary endpoint of helping patients to fall asleep faster in a Phase 3 study of delayed sleep-wake phase disorder. The second was VQW-765, a “negative” for Vanda, according to Oppenheimer.
The third late-stage readout that the analysts have their eye on is for Nereus—also known as tradipitant—an oral motion-sickness drug that received approval in late December 2025. Vanda is now testing Nereus for GLP-1-induced vomiting. The biotech launched a Phase 3 trial in April, with topline data slated for the fourth quarter.
Phase 2 data reported in November last year showed that tradipitant significantly lowered the proportion of patients with vomiting—the trial’s primary endpoint—as compared to placebo. The study involved 116 patients who were pretreated with tradipitant or placebo before being given a 1-mg injection of Novo’s Wegovy.
Aside from the trio of late-stage readouts, Oppenheimer said Vanda’s “near-term story” will also now depend on launch execution for the schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder drug Bysanti, which notched regulatory clearance in February, and the FDA’s verdict for Quimilza in generalized pustular psoriasis expected by mid- December .

Westport Fuel Systems Inc. changed its name to Aetherion Technologies Inc. on Thursday. The Vancouver, British Columbia, company said its next push is bringing Cespira’s high-pressure direct injection (HPDI) fuel system to North American long-haul fleets on compressed natural gas .
The rename follows Westport’s July 2025 sale of its light-duty business to an investment vehicle of Netherlands-based Heliaca Investments for a base price of $79.5 million. A company brand sheet ties the new name to that divestiture and to the transfer of the Westport name.
Aetherion’s chief executive said the rename tells the market who the company is after a strategy reset that narrowed what it works on.
“The bread and butter is the original foundation of the company, the original technology, HPDI, high pressure direct injection,” said Dan Sceli, CEO of Aetherion, in an interview with FreightWaves. “That’s really how it all started and that’s the core that we want to get back to focusing on and not trying to do 20 things part way, but do a couple of things really well.”
The name draws on two Greek roots, according to the company: aithēr, the clean air of the upper sky, and ion, meaning motion or energy.
Shareholders approved a name change at the company’s June 30 annual and special meeting. The company expects its shares to trade under the new name on the Toronto Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, subject to final exchange approvals, on a date it has not announced.
HPDI anchors the renamed company
Philip Hill co-founded Westport in 1995 and invented HPDI, which keeps the diesel engine and changes the fuel it burns. HPDI is sold through Cespira, a joint venture with Volvo Group launched in 2024. Aetherion owns 55% and Volvo owns 45%.
HPDI runs in more than 12,000 trucks worldwide, according to the company. Cespira posted second-quarter revenue of $27.1 million, up 125% from $12 million a year earlier, according to Westport’s second-quarter management’s discussion and analysis , dated Aug. 11.
The open question now, he said, is how quickly fleets switch to natural gas for its stable pricing.
“There’s lots of places for battery electric and fuel cells, but not on these long-haul truck fleets,” he said.
HPDI can also run hydrogen and natural gas blends on the same core technology, Sceli said. Most of hydrogen’s cost is tied up in liquefying and transporting it, he said, and it needs to get closer to $5 an equivalent gallon to compete. He sees blending hydrogen into existing U.S. natural gas pipelines as one way around that cost.
“They’ve been doing it in Hawaii for 50 years,” he said.
Hawaiʻi Gas blends up to 15% hydrogen into the synthetic natural gas it makes at a plant built in 1974 and distributes by pipeline on Oʻahu.
Cespira and Volvo signed a development agreement in June to run Volvo’s 13-liter engine on hydrogen through HPDI, with a European commercial launch targeted before 2030, according to Westport’s second-quarter filing.
CNG storage for North America
Cespira’s growth so far has come on liquefied natural gas, Sceli said. North America is the next market, he said, and its fuel is compressed natural gas, with pipelines and infrastructure already in place.
Westport showed a CNG demonstration truck at ACT Expo in May, a Volvo VNL 300 on a high-pressure storage system. The company reported more than 600 miles of range and up to 10 miles per gallon equivalent on that truck. Sceli said a number of large fleets have shown interest, and Volvo is working through its business case for the system in North America. He told FreightWaves in April that Environmental Protection Agency certification is the primary step toward commercialization.
Fleets want price stability on top of savings, Sceli said.
“They want to know that six months or 12 months down the road, what their fuel pricing is going to be,” he said. “This volatility in diesel causes headaches for all of these fleets and pricing and dealing with short- and long-term contracts.”
Over the next six to 12 months, Sceli said, the two things to watch are Cespira’s growth and the CNG system.
“Westport is bringing a new CNG storage system to combine it with HPDI for the North American market, because the market is looking for an alternative and we have it,” he said.

More companies are increasing their use of used pallets , according to Modern Materials Handling’s annual pallet survey , with 35% of respondents saying they use more than a year ago. In the previous survey, 18% reported an increase.
The findings come from the 2026 Pallet Market Evaluation, produced by Peerless Research Group . The survey included 115 MMH readers who work at locations that use pallets.
Many respondents already use wood pallets in their day-to-day operations. Nearly three-quarters (73%) use used or core wood pallets, while 52% purchase new wood pallets, with some companies using both.
Most respondents have kept their use of used pallets steady: 59% reported no change from a year earlier. Just 6% are using fewer, down from 22% in the previous survey.
RELATED: Read Modern Materials Handling’s 2026 Pallet Market Evaluation
Quality and availability remain concerns
Among companies buying used pallets, 37% say quality is not as good as with new pallets. Another 22% report fewer available pallets or shortages, while 13% say used wood pallets have become more expensive.
Still, these experiences aren't universal. One-third of used-pallet buyers say they haven't encountered those problems and don't expect future purchasing difficulties.
Getting pallets returned is another concern raised in the report. “Usually, I don’t get the pallets back,” one survey participant said, pointing to a recurring need to replace pallets that leave an operation and never return.
Wood remains the top choice
Wood pallets remain in use at 92% of surveyed companies, unchanged from 2025. The standard 48-by-40-inch pallet is the most common size, used by 73% of respondents.
Plastic pallets gained ground, with 36% of respondents using them, up from 28% last year. Companies can use several materials, so those figures include operations using both wood and plastic.
Pallet pooling also grew to 19% of respondents, up from 16% in the previous survey. Vendors also provide other services: 38% of respondents use on-site recycling and reclamation management, up from 32% last year.

The Port of Savannah has won federal approval for a $2.3 billion container terminal that will add room to handle 3.5 million more twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) a year. Construction is scheduled to begin in January 2028.
What’s Related
Georgia Ports Authority President Kevin Price announced the permit approval on October 14 during the annual State of the Port of Savannah event. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers approved the Savannah Container Terminal permit after a three-year review.
The new terminal will cover 350 acres on Hutchison Island in Savannah and is expected to be completed in the mid-2030s. Georgia Ports says the facility will be able to handle the largest container ships .
“We’re excited about the Savannah Container Terminal’s role in our future growth and investment plans to take us to a 12 million TEU gateway container port, serving customers in Georgia and our nation with the best infrastructure in a high-growth region,” Price said.
RELATED: Top 30 U.S. Ports Ranked By Container Imports
More room for containers
Savannah can currently handle 7.75 million TEUs annually, according to Georgia Ports. The authority says its planned expansion projects will bring that figure to 12 million TEUs.
The Hutchison Island project is one part of that work. Georgia Ports is also spending $1.6 billion to upgrade Ocean Terminal, increasing its annual container handling limit from 200,000 TEUs to 1.75 million TEUs.
That project is expected to be completed by the end of 2028, several years before the new Savannah Container Terminal opens. The two projects will give Savannah additional space to handle containers on separate construction schedules.
A larger port investment plan
Georgia Ports Chairman Alec Poitevint said the authority plans to invest $5 billion in future port infrastructure, following $4.13 billion spent over the past decade on port and inland infrastructure. The new container terminal is part of that longer-term spending plan.
“We play the long game here,” Poitevint said.
Price also discussed the Talmadge Bridge, plans to widen and deepen Savannah Harbor, and the Gainesville Inland Port. Those projects were among the port and inland transportation updates presented alongside the newly approved terminal.

Credit Port of Houston
By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
15 October 2026
Elevated import volumes have strained drayage capacity at US container gateways.
Much of the recent spotlight has been on the port of Houston, which is handling record volumes of cargo, and traffic is expected to keep growing, fuelled by multiple drivers.
Since mid-August US trucking and logistics firms have blamed tight drayage capacity as the biggest brake on growth and warned of bottlenecks at ports and inland rail ramps. The biggest factor has been the tightening trucking sector, exacerbated by a seasonal shift of drivers from drayage to the longhaul sector, in response to peak volumes.
This year’s peak season has lasted longer than usual, owing to uncertainty over tariffs and front-loading to beat higher fuel surcharges. According to Descartes, US imports of containerised cargo were up 10.3% year on year (YoY) in September.
By late August the National Drayage Spot Market Index was up 8.2% YoY. By the beginning of this month this had climbed to 9.8%, and the national drayage demand index was 18% higher than the past six months and 9% above the previous four weeks.
Various sources have reported higher-than-average increases in drayage rates from Houston. According to data provider Drayrates, they were up 34% on a year earlier, whereas the national average was +18%.
Paul Brashier, VP of global supply chain at ITS Logistics, an Echo company, reported that dray rates in Houston had shot up 40% over the past four months – albeit from a low base.
He was not surprised; he had already warned about the build-up of traffic through the port late last year and flagged the gateway as a pain point a month ago.
He pointed to a convergence of factors that have boosted traffic through Houston: record container volume for the first half of this year, with its teu count up 3% YoY; through August loaded imports were up about 5% YoY, with traffic from Asia up nearly 12%; and imports have surged because of rapid expansion of manufacturing in Texas and the tidal wave of equipment and materials for the build-out of AI-related infrastructure in the state. At the same time exports of resins have jumped, as the hostilities in the Middle East have disrupted exports from that region.
Other dynamics have added to the momentum on the import side. Over the past 45 days, some cargo owners have apparently booked transatlantic routings via the US Gulf coast to avoid congestion at the Panama Canal, Mr Brashier noted. He added that concerns over large volumes of imports stretching dwell times at the California container gateways had prompted cargo owners to move some imports through Houston instead. Moreover, the volume of containers entering the port en route to Mexico had grown, he added.
The port of Houston has also been the most prominent maritime gateway for outsize and project cargo for the US, which has added to the rise in volumes leaving the port on the land side, mostly for the build-up of manufacturing in Texas and work to beef up the US power grid infrastructure. Some of the logistics providers that specialise in this sector feel encroachment from the container business.
“Now there are containers everywhere at the port,” said one project forwarder executive.
The National Retail Federation recently signalled that the extended peak season should be winding down this month, as most of the holiday merchandise had arrived. Containerised imports at the major US box ports are forecast to add up to 25.8m teu for the full year, an increase of 1.4% from 2025.
The anticipated waning of retail imports will alleviate some of the pressure at Houston, but the other drivers of volume are showing no signs of slowing. Mr Brashier is bracing himself for further volume growth going forward.
“Houston is adding another [container] terminal. That speaks volumes to what they see on the horizon,” he said.
ITS has expanded its footprint at the port over the past three years, and will continue to do so, trying to keep up with demand, he added.
Despite the increase in throughput and the diminished driver pool, the situation has not stymied flows from the port to the interior, Mr Brashier said.
“We’re not seeing a significant amount of dwell,” he reported. “The port and the ecosystem, and the chassis, seem to be pretty resilient. It’s just not having enough trucking capacity.”
He advised cargo owners to strengthen and expand their relationships with drayage providers, and to make early arrangements for capacity and chassis equipment, especially when it comes to special cargo, like hazmat or reefers.
“If you haven’t upped capacity, do that now because the market continues to grow,” he warned.

BMW put the new i3 to the test to showcase the power of its Gen6 batteries. The long-wheelbase i3 covered 753 miles (1,213 km) without stopping, the longest covered by any BMW EV to date.
BMW i3 50L delivers 1,213 km of range on a single charge
BMW Group began series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) EV batteries in Shenyang on October 15, its third global production site for the new battery tech.
To prove the power of its latest battery tech, set to power its Neue Klasse lineup, BMW put the new i3 50L through an endurance test to see how far it can really drive.
BMW said the new cylindrical cells offer over 20% higher energy density, enabling 30% faster charging and longer driving range than the previous generation.

After unveiling the i3 50L, a long-wheelbase version developed specifically for China at the Chengdu Auto Show in August, BMW said it would deliver a CLTC range of over 621 miles (1,000 km), topping the iX3 50L with a CLTC range of 571 miles (919 km).
During the event, the i3 50L managed over 753 miles (1,213 km) on a single charge, a new record for a BMW electric vehicle, the company said. The electric sedan achieved an extremely efficient 8.8 kWh per 100 km, covering highways, city and rural streets.
While BMW said it was a brand record, not a global one, it was enough to top the Mercedes Vision EQXX, which traveled 1,202 km from Germany to the UK in 2022.
In June, BMW drove an iX3 50L prototype over 500 miles (800 km) around the Qinghai Lake grand loop. It achieved an energy consumption of 12.6 kWh per 100 km.
The BMW iX3 Long Wheelbase (left) and i3 Long Wheelbase (right) Source: BMW
The long-wheelbase i3 uses a 113.4 kWh battery that delivers a CLTC range of over 621 miles (1,000 km). Thanks to its 800V architecture, the i3 50L can add 248 miles (400 km) of range in 10 minutes with up to 400 kW fast charging.
BMW opened orders for the iX3 50L at the Chengdu Auto Show in August, starting at RMB 269,900 ($40,000). The i3 50L is expected to go on sale later this year, with customer deliveries set to begin in the first quarter of 2027.
In the US, the 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive is now available to order , starting at $61,500. It has an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 434 miles.
The 2027 BMW i3 is also on sale starting at the same price of $61,500. The electric sedan delivers up to 468 miles of range.

In this webinar, BioSpace will gathered experts to discuss China’s impact on the future of biotech and how both U.S. and Chinese companies can thrive—and maybe even collaborate.
Register to watch
Depending on who you ask, China is a well of biotech innovation or an existential threat to U.S. dominance in the industry. Big Pharma can’t seem to get enough of the therapies being pumped out by myriad biotechs in China, while U.S.-based companies are struggling to find their role in this new paradigm.
In this webinar, BioSpace will gathered experts to discuss China’s impact on the future of biotech and how both U.S. and Chinese companies can thrive—and maybe even collaborate.
Featured Speakers
Lila Hope
Partner | Sidley
Lila Hope represents biotechnology, pharmaceutical, medical technology, diagnostics, vaccine, and digital health companies in strategic transactions across the life sciences sector. Her practice focuses on complex licensing, collaboration, co-development, option, platform discovery, commercialization, supply, and other commercial agreements that support the discovery, development, and commercialization of innovative products and technologies. Lila advises clients on a broad range of partnering and transactional matters involving intellectual property, business, operational, and regulatory considerations. She regularly structures and negotiates complex strategic collaborations between emerging and established life sciences companies, including platform and discovery collaborations, option-based transactions, and commercial arrangements supporting clinical development and product commercialization. She also counsels management, business development, legal, and operational teams on day-to-day transactional matters and risk assessment.
Patroski Lawson
Founder | KPM Group
Patroski founded KPM Group after 25+ years of government affairs experience spanning the public and private sectors. Patroski spent over 20 years leading government affairs for three global healthcare companies: Solvay Pharmaceuticals, Abbott, and Lundbeck, lobbying and advocating across Brussels, Washington D.C., and state capitols nationwide. He developed strategic plans, managed multimillion-dollar budgets, and advised U.S. and global CEOs on policy, risk management, stakeholder engagement, and PAC strategy. At Solvay, he was instrumental in securing a $300 million federal contract from HHS to build the first cell-based influenza vaccine facility in the U.S. Patroski founded KPM Group to bring that same strategic expertise to emerging biotech companies navigating the complexities of government affairs, legislative advocacy, and policy engagement. A 2014 graduate of the Public Affairs Institute and former Executive Committee member of the Public Affairs Council, Patroski has been a featured speaker at the National PAC Conference and co-hosted the Innovate to Motivate Political Involvement Professionals Conference. Patroski is the co-founder of The Just Society and the Rare Disease Company Coalition (RDCC) , as well as the founder of American Biotech Innovation Alliance (ABIA) . Outside of work, Patroski is a Certified Specialist of Wine (CSW) and founder of the Executive Wine Lunch Society (EWLS).
Jeremy Levin
Co-Founder and Executive Chair | Ovid Therapeutics
Jeremy Levin, D.Phil., MB BChir, is co-founder and executive chairman of Ovid Therapeutics, a public company developing novel medicines to treat epilepsies and seizure-related disorders. Levin is concurrently chairman of Opthea. Prior to founding Ovid, Levin was president and CEO of Teva Pharmaceutical Industries. Before Teva, he was a member of the executive committee of Bristol-Myers Squibb, where he was the architect, lead and implementer of the String of Pearls strategy, which transformed the company and helped catalyze the modern immuno-oncology era in the biopharmaceutical industry. Levin joined Bristol-Myers Squibb from Novartis, where he served as global head of strategic alliances. He has also served on the boards of multiple public biopharmaceutical companies, including Biocon and Lundbeck. Levin currently serves on the board and executive committee of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization as past chairman. He was named one of the 25 most influential biotechnology leaders by Fierce Biotech , recognized among the leading biotechnology CEOs by The Healthcare Technology Report and selected as a PharmaVoice100 CEO in 2020 and 2021. In 2021, Endpoints named him one of the 60 living pioneers of the biotechnology industry. He is the recipient of the Albert Einstein Award for Leadership in Life Sciences and the B’nai B’rith Award for Distinguished Achievement. In June 2020, he edited and published the bestseller Biotechnology in the Time of Covid-19 . His recent book, Biotech in the Balance: Saving a Strategic Industry in an Age of Distrust , was published on May 19, 2026. Levin has written and spoken extensively on biotechnology, scientific innovation, capital formation and the role of biotechnology as a strategic national capability.
Jake Becraft
CEO and Co-Founder | Strand Therapeutics
Jake Becraft is the CEO and co-founder of Strand Therapeutics, and serves on its Board of Directors. Together with colleagues at MIT’s renowned Synthetic Biology Center, he led the development of the world’s first synthetic biology programming language for mRNA. He serves on the board of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO) and the Massachusetts Biotechnology Council (MassBio). Jake received his Ph.D. in Biological Engineering and Synthetic Biology from MIT. Beyond Strand, Jake has become one of biotech’s visible voices on U.S. clinical trial policy, testifying before the U.S. House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and writing in The Washington Post on expanding patient access to first-in-human trials. Previously, he also served as a Science and Technology advisor to legislators in the Massachusetts State Legislature.
Annalee Armstrong
Senior Editor

1970 "Chevelle SS" 454 Wagon Is an Eight-People Muscle Car, Looks and Drives Like a 400-HP Dream
33 photos
Photo: Pedal To The Metal
In 1970, Chevrolet introduced the 454 big-block motor, following a generic Detroit trend that saw an unprecedented (and never since succeeded) cubic-inch inflation of megalithic proportions. As a sidenote: Cadillac one-upped everyone with its 500-cube motor, also launched that year. Chevrolet, on the other hand, dropped the big-block in intermediates and wagons and pretty much anything above compact and pony. So here we are in 2026, watching a Dutch gearhead review a Chevelle 454 wagon on the road.
“Hold on a minute, the Chevelle wagon didn’t have a 454 from the factory!” I hear you loud and crystal-clear, Bowtie fans. It didn’t/ I know I said the Chevy wagons did carry the mighty big-block, but those were the full-sizers, the 119-inch-wheelsbased longroofs. The Chevelle was an A-body platform, 116 inches between the front and rear wheel hubs. Those three extra inches made the Brookwoods, Townsmans, and Kingwoods worthy of the full beans.
The Nomad, Greenbrier, and Concours, meanwhile, had to settle for 402 cubic inches at the most. Those were the wagons built on the Chevelle platform, and were kept outside the select Super Sport circles, were the 454 felt right at home. So, how did this mid-size wagon end up with SS badges, and a 454 underhood? Take a wild guess. I’m thinking someone did the right thing, and made what Chevrolet should’ve, but didn’t.
Impressive? You bet! Just play the first video embedded down below, and listen to the ecstatic car nut describing the odd-ball Chevy. And he’s not at all easy to impress – not when it comes to cars. AutoTopNL, the YouTube outlet where Max Beelaerts tests and reviews the meanest, baddest, fastest concoctions devised by Homo Sapiens Pistonicus, is solid proof of the man’s sound understanding of performance cars. And yet…
Photo: Pedal To The Metal Courtesy of the merry-go-muscle gearheads from Pedal to the Metal Muscle Cars in Sneek, the Netherlands, ("a candy store if you are into American muscle cars," as Beelaerts describes it), this car is very much real. A 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle wagon is how the YouTuber introduces the car, although that’s technically incorrect – the Chevelle nameplate didn’t land on wagons, even though it was basically the same thing with a bigger passenger space.
In this particular case, eight-occupancy capacity is quite a lot. The third, rear-facing bench seat is one super-cool feature in cars – and American wagons from that era proudly displayed that particularity. It’s what we’d nowadays refer to as a “soccer mom’s ride,” except it’s a dad wagon. A dad power wagon, because 454 cubic inches aren’t just for filling up the engine bay, and emptying the fuel tank.
Wearing a fresh white repaint with metallic blue stripes, the 208-inch (5.25-meter) power cruiser very gently hints at what’s lurking underhood via subtle “454” fender badges. “Absolutely massive 8-seat muscle car, so freaking cool," Beelaerts marvels. I like – and share – his opinion. 8-seat muscle car. Chevrolet didn’t go all in, unfortunately, back in the day, and didn’t drop the meanest big-block into mid-sizers.
Photo: Pedal To The Metal Only the big wagons – built on the full-size platform – had the optional motor, tuned to 345 hp (LS1), or 390 hp (LS5). Yes, the same LS5 that was good for only 360 horses in the Chevelle SS 454. “Only.” The LS6 wasn’t allowed anywhere near a tailgated body, but still; 390 horsepower for a grocery-getter was no joke.
Pedal to the Metal thought for a minute, and posthumously righted a historical wrong. They dropped the big-block in the medium wagon. They also poured fresh chrome on the pointy grille, front bumper, headlight bezels, mirrors, moldings, and emblems, and fitted new weatherstripping, side marker lenses, and crisp taillight lenses.
Tapping the solid metal door handles, Beelaerts grins, "Just listen to all this hardware, it's like a proper car, not like the plastic ($%|7) boxes that we get to drive these days." Out back, the factory double-acting tailgate features a power window actuated via the key or dashboard switch, swinging open like a door or dropping flat. Climbing inside over the bumper step, Beelaerts tests the nostalgic, foldable, rear-facing third bench.
Photo: Pedal To The Metal Sitting backwards in the cargo bay immediately sparks an idea for the Dutch reviewer, who plays soccer (football, for the rest of the world) on Sundays. This would be a cool team ride – albeit with room for only eight adults. Originally, this California-built wagon led a much quieter life.
This genuine four-door, three-seat V8 station wagon rolled off the General Motors assembly line in Los Angeles, California, originally powered by a 307-cubic-inch small-block V8. Pedal to the Metal later transformed the cruiser in-house, dropping in a freshly rebuilt 400-hp, 7,439-cc, 7.4-liter, 454-cubic-inch big-block V8. "This is an engine that doesn't belong in the car," Beelaerts notes, "but it is so freaking cool."
Under the hood, the 454 V8 pairs an Edelbrock intake, Holley Sniper Electronic Fuel Injection , and upgraded ignition system with performance headers and a custom-built exhaust (with headers). A rebuilt 3-speed automatic transmission with a new torque converter and Gear Vendors overdrive sends power to a 3.55:1 rear axle. By splitting each gear ratio in half, the overdrive creates six effective speeds, giving drivers "a bit more cruising comfort on the highway."
Photo: Pedal To The Metal Power front disc brakes hide behind 15-inch wheels wrapped in 245 Cooper Cobra Radial G/T tires, while the underbody boasts cavity wax protection, a new fuel tank, new fuel lines, and parking brake system. "It sounds freaking glorious, it runs really well, and it feels almost restomod," Beelaerts explains, praising how those updates let you drive "worry-free" instead of "driving butt-clenched because you're worried that it might stop working."
Inside the beautifully preserved blue cabin, Vintage Air air conditioning, a custom steering wheel (a bit too small, if you ask me), a Sniper EFI display, and extra gauges for oil temperature, water temperature, and oil pressure join lap belts that Beelaerts jokes are " basically there to hold you in place after you have an accident so they don't have to go and find you." Still, sliding across the wide 3-seater front bench stirs a deep emotional chord.
"I have a physical reaction to these cars when I drive it, and even though I know that it's not realistic to be driving this every day, I just yearn for it," Beelaerts confesses. Picturing his wife sitting beside him after they discussed buying a 3-seat front-bench car just the week before filming, he laughs, "My mind immediately went to a Fiat Multipla, of course, but this is a slightly cooler option."
Photo: Pedal To The Metal Twisting the key awakens all 7.4 liters of Detroit muscle . "The entire car shakes, and it just feels like it's so powerful and ready to go, and eager to go," Beelaerts beams, pulling onto the road with "very, very powerful and very, very torquey" thrust.
Wafting effortlessly over Dutch village speed bumps without feeling like an unwieldy pickup, the Chevelle inspires pure joy: "It has so much aura, this thing." Yup, that’s what the 454 was built for – aura. And realigning chakras in rivals from 1970, with terrifying acceleration, courtesy of 500 lb-ft of torque.
"You think that you're not cool because you're a dad and you drive a station wagon? Well, think again, I need it!" Beelaerts exclaims. The YouTuber concludes by calling the cruiser “an antidote to everything that I don't like about modern cars." If ever there was a definition of automotive redemption, Max nailed it in the head.
Photo: Pedal To The Metal That thrill echoes 1970, a landmark year when General Motors lifted its 400-cubic-inch midsize cap and Chevrolet introduced the 454-cubic-inch V8 to replace the short-lived 427-cubic-inch V8 launched in 1966. While Chevelle SS buyers got the 360-hp LS5 or 450-hp LS6 454 in coupes, convertibles, and El Caminos (plus Monte Carlos, the new-for-the-year Personal Luxury Coupe), wagons had to settle for smaller powerplants.
Midsize long-roof buyers instead started with a 155-hp, 250-cubic-inch Turbo-Thrift inline-six or a base 200-hp, 307-cubic-inch small-block V8. Stepping up unlocked two 350-cubic-inch V8s producing 250 hp with a two-barrel carburetor or 300 hp in four-barrel trim, while the range-topping Chevelle wagon engine was a 330-hp, 402-cubic-inch big-block V8 (the punched-out 396-CID V8 of 1965-1969).
Photo: Pedal To The Metal Out of 442,046 Chevelle passenger cars built for the pivotal model year (or 489,582 including El Caminos), wagons totaled 40,612 units, split into 5,634 inline-6s and 34,978 V8s. 11,466 were entry-level Nomads, 8,178 came as Greenbriers, and 14,915 had the Concours trim. The headcount was completed by 6,053 Concours Estates, the best-optioned mid-size chevy wagons of 1970.
This particular example is a one-of-none mongrel, but one that kept the best traits of its parents, pairing the torque titan 454 big-block V8 with the spacious body of the Chevelle-based station wagon. Sure, the SS badges on the grille will tell anyone that it’s a custom build, but it’s a tasteful execution. Best thing about it? You can buy it. Pedal to the metal is asking a very reasonable €49,750 for it – approximately 55,800 bucks at the mid-October, 2026 exchange rate – with 7,850 miles on the clock.

Not an Optical Illusion: Four Differently Sized Bentley Blowers Come Together for the First Time
14 photos
Photo: Bentley
I’m pretty sure every single day something comes along to trick your eyes and brains. The images we have here, showing the historically important Bentley Blower in no less than four different sizes, are not that, as this is not an optical illusion, but an actual gathering of Blowers inspired by a piece of engineering from long ago.
There’s a big chance most of you now reading this know what the Blower is all about. Officially titled the 1929 Bentley 4½-liter, the supercharged machine was one of four Bentleys created for racing purposes on the tracks of the Old Continent, including at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1930.
Team Car No. 2, with registration number UU 5872 was the source of inspiration for the creation of its smaller siblings you can see in the photos attached to this text. One of them is the Bentley Blower Jnr road legal scale car that was first announced three years ago by Hedley Studios (formerly known as The Little Car Company), and the other two much smaller replicas put together by Amalgam Collection.
We’ve discussed the Jnr several times since it was first announced, the last time in spring of last year, when Bentley and Hedley announced the start of production. Now, more than a year after that time, the British companies took the opportunity to let us all know that the initial run of 25 scale Blowers are ready to be delivered to their owners.
Photo: Bentley This vehicle is an 85 percent scale version of the original Blower, powered by a fully electric powertrain that delivers 31 hp and is capable of carrying the slammer car to a top speed of 50 mph (80 kph). The maximum range the car can travel on a single charge is 75 miles (120 km).
The above numbers are not set in stone, as they vary depending on region and local regulations. Over in Europe, for instance, the top speed is limited to 45 mph (72 kph), while over in the U.S. it is capped at 25 mph (40 kph). Naturally, there are no restrictions when it comes to range,
The 25 Jnrs that have already been made are part of a limited run of 349 that will ever be produced, with the very first one already delivered to Bentley’s headquarters in Crewe. Each of these scale cars is said to cost around $120,000 – which is pennies, if you consider the fact that the original it is based on is valued at around $34 million.
The other two replicas of the Blower, made by Amalgam Collection, are not as impressive as the Jnr, of course, and that’s owed to the fact that they are not only smaller, but also far less mechanically complex.
Photo: Bentley There are two Amalgam variants available, a 1:18 one and a 1:8 variant that has been around for six years already. The former is the newest addition to the range, as is the race-weathered version that accompanies them.
Despite their size, the tiny Blowers are not to be taken lightly. Bentley describes one of the two toys (Amalgam might resent that term, but that is what they are, if you really think about it), the 1:18 version, as the most technically accomplished model Amalgam has ever made.
What these scale models lack in terms of, well, everything when compared to the Jnr, they make up in exclusivity. Owners of the Blower Continuation Series cars can have either one of the two scale replicas configured and crafted in such a way as to mirror the full-size cars.
Despite their very small size, the two scale Blowers are not exactly cheap to own. The 1:18 version sells at the time of writing for $1,595, while the larger 1:8 model carries a sticker that reads $26,995.
Photo: Bentley When it comes to the race-weathered version of its 1:8 scale model, Amalgam will only make 30 of them, and each will be hand-painted in such a way that they recreate as faithfully as possible the dirt, patina, and battle scars a car usually gains in the heat of the race.
More specifically, the design of these 30 units mirrors the look of Team Car No.2 after its 1930 presence at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. That includes, believe it or not, the bent rear fenders that resulted from tire failures.
Despite its intentional battle scars, this version of the most expensive Bentley in Amalgam’s collection is selling for at least $27,875 at the time of writing.
As for the car that inspired the three differently sized replicas, Team Car No. 2 is no longer actively racing, but that doesn’t mean it’s completely idle in a garage somewhere. Now part of the Bentley Heritage Collection, it makes appearances at various events across the world, including the ones that involve actual driving.
