Ridden: Macfox's X1S Commuter E-Bike Surprises With Sturdy and Customizable Build at $1,400
46 photos
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution
One of the benefits of writing for autoevolution is that I often have the pleasure of testing all sorts of vehicles. One of the industries I often research is e-biking, and this time around we’ll be diving into an e-bikes dubbed the X1S from Macfox, a brand that I'm not testing for the second time, and if I may, I continue to be pleasantly surprised.
Folks, the name Macfox is one that we’ve shed light upon before, when we tested their oversized X7L e-bike earlier this year. They have, however, shown signs of life as early as 2022, and since then, have slowly crept into home after home with their solid and accessible rides.
Pleased with the free press review that we completed on the X7L , Macfox asked me to give one of their entry-level models a go, in particular, the X1S, a bike that bears a similar frame to the X7L, but a bit smaller. However, as I would soon find out, smaller does not mean any less capable, and the X1S actually surprised me in several ways.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution Before going on, however, allow me to point out that I had the occasion to test the European version as I'm currently stationed out here, awaiting to attend EICMA in Milan. So the specs and what we learned about the X1S will differ a bit from what US-destined versions can achieve.
Design Evaluation As one of the smaller e-bikes from Macfox, the X1S distinguishes itself from the X7L with a smaller frame and wheels that are tighter too. Instead of 5-inch rubbers that the X7L exhibited, the X1S has 4-inch tires, and a tread that’s more inclined for tarmac instead of dirt roads and trails. That, however, doesn’t mean it won’t feel at home on a dirt road, it does, put you’ll need to be a bit wearier of punctures.
The frame on the other hand, is still one that resembles the whole scrambler style of rides, and oddly enough, in a good way. It actually feels a bit motorcycle-like on the turns due to its trail and head tube angle; we’ll talk more about that shortly.
The seat is also an elongated one, and since there is a set of foot pegs on this one, just like on the X7L, two riders can enjoy a trip. Macfox mentions a peak rider weight of 100 kg (220 lbs), but I did try and push this limit with a friend and I, and even at 125 kg (276 lbs), the X1S still moved, albeit a bit sluggishly.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution The frame also never ceases to amaze me in terms of build quality. From the first few minutes on the X1S, I remarked just how sturdy the backbone is. It just feels solid, and there’s no doubt about it. It’s steel, so it does weigh a bit; Macfox mentions a weight of 30 kg (66 lbs) for this thing.
One other aspect of this sort of frame that you do need to consider, especially if you’re a taller rider, is the inability to modify seat height. As a result, pedaling on this style of e-bike can be a bit uncomfortable, and often, they are equipped with throttle so you can just sit back and enjoy the ride. The X1S does have throttle functionality, and it does play a crucial role in our ability to do wheelies with this one.
However, I had a bit of a different experience with the throttle function because in Europe, Macfox limits its use to just 6 kph (3.7 mph) and is very strict on sharing the information needed to unlock the full capability of the bike. Most likely, there are folks in your town that know how to unlock these babies, or you can find instructions online.
For the sake of the review, I didn’t tamper with this aspect of the bike, as that’s how Macfox sells it in the EU, and frankly, I don’t mind much. It does make it a bit difficult to stay in the saddle for more than 20 km (12 mph) at a time before you need to stretch those legs.
For Europe, the X1S is also limited to a peak of a nice and legal 25 kph, but for the US, it’s limited to 20 mph (32 kph), so plenty of speed to get around town, and in NA, throttle use is unrestricted, so enjoy.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution Another important change that applies to European models is the motor strength. Nominally, it runs at 250 W, whereas, US models include a 500 W motor, both are strapped to the rear hub and both versions are said to peak at 750 W.
What I was unable to find for European versions is torque output, but what I can say is that the X1S had no trouble tackling 15-degree hills in my area, even with the single-speed drivetrain setup, another reason why throttle use would be fantastic on this version and why we can really sit in the saddle for too long.
For riders in the US, the X1S does boast a peak of 65 Nm (48 lb-ft) of torque.
This brings us to range, a wildly controversial side of any e-bike ride, mainly because of the countless different aspects that affect each ride. Yet, for the X1S, we’re told that a peak of 50 km (31 miles) is the max range here, yet my experience was a wildly different one, and in the best way possible; I also know why I pulled the number I did.
In terms of suspension, the X1S is only sporting a front fork with a reported 120 mm of travel, ample room for bump-absorbing action, which is essential considering that it’s not an adjustable fork, at least, not the version I was riding. Other X1S models do appear to have adjustability, so it depends on the model year, who you get it from, and if any modifications have been made.
Speaking of which, Macfox designs the bike as a whole to be highly customizable, and with countless accessories online and even on their website, we can create more than just an X1S, you can make your OWN X1S, as unique as you.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution The last traits of the design that I need to mention include the headlight at the front, the trigger for the rear light – it even has turn signals but no actual lights – and the most important, disc brakes with hydraulic pistons and calipers that seem a bit overkill for the discs but help stop on a gosh darned dime if needed. Toss on a couple of fenders, and you’re off.
Ride Time In terms of the riding experience, things were actually rather surprising. I had ridden scrambler/bobber-style e-bikes before, and this is one of the ones that I found rather decent in terms of comfort. While the frame style does force your legs to never fully extend, if we shuffle back on the seat a bit, we can access a bit more legroom.
Since the throttle doesn’t help out on European versions, keep in mind that the specs I'll be pointing out are based solely on pedal assist.
Since legroom has a whole lot to do with comfort , I'll continue there before heading into more important territory. The front suspension on the X1S is, as you’d expect from 120 mm of travel, it is squishy, but the rear could use some shocks, especially if you hit some larger cracks, come off a curb, or anything or the sort. But, to reduce vibrations from the tarmac and even handle hardpack dirt roads with small gravel, it’s fine.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution You can tamper with tire pressure to play around with some softness, at the cost of range, that is. The tires do play a pivotal role in softening up the road on such a burly frame.
One aspect of riding this e-bike that I found rather interesting is the way it takes turns. Much like a motorcycle, or at least, the one’s I've ridden, once you commit to a corner, the bike takes over and does the work for you, which makes it rather easy to turn, but you do need to be making a conscious decision to turn as it’ll pull you in the direction you’re going. I like it.
In terms of how much abuse and vibrations the whole system can take, here too i was pleased, with the frame really feeling solid on any terrain I tested. Nothing bangs around and makes wild noises either, except the occasional brake pad touching the disc where torsional forces may be too much for the spoke layup. It is a steel frame, so it will bend a bit but can take quite the abuse.
Lately, there has been a renewed interest in steel tubing for bikes, and countless brands are now crafting nothing but steel bikes, be they custom or mass-produced. It’s inexpensive and easy to work with, but a dash heavy, as we all know.
Onto the more important aspects such as power and range. First off, I mentioned that a 250 W motor is in place here, and since I was only riding with pedal assist, it’s difficult for me to tell you a precise acceleration time. However, in third speed, the one that allows us to access all the power from this motor, I was reaching 25 kph in around 10-12 seconds or so. I do weight around 77 kg (170 lbs) and sometimes, I was off to a rough start.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution What I can mention is that if the throttle was working, that time could be reduced drastically, and would make it easier to enjoy a ride with a friend on the rear, if you don’t overload the bike too much.
Yet, throttle function would also greatly influence how much range we can squeeze out of the 13 Ah battery (48 V ecosystem). Keep in mind that Macfox mentions a peak of just 50 km for the European version, but somehow, I was experiencing a whole lot more, and as mentioned, I know why: the lack of throttle.
As such, I was always in pedal assist mode, and usually, in the second of the three speed settings, staying at around 20 kph on average. This, somehow, granted access to an average of over 50 km, 55-60 km (up to 37 miles), but that is on a full charge. If I stayed at 10-15% before recharging, yes, 50 km is a clearly on the menu.
Keep in mind that the X1S can be equipped with another battery as well, allowing us to double our riding time and possibly use it for delivery services.
Recharging such a big battery does, usually take a while, and in the X1S’ case, up to six hours is what you’ll have to wait for before riding out again. But, if you recharge your battery after riding, you’ll never have to experience that sort of downtime.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution This battery is a removable one, which does help if you live on the upper levels of an apartment building; elevators need to be big to fit this inside too, and you can do so in a vertical position with some light acrobatics.
Since the drivetrain is one aspect that I had mixed feelings about, I want to take a moment and mention the importance of having some gearing available. A single-speed setup is not optimum for tackling hills, and while I could make it up any in my town, on some of them, you can hear the motor struggle a bit. Speaking of struggle, I was surprised at how much quieter the X1S motor is in comparison to the X7L. Sometimes, the treads on the tarmac make more noise.
What I noticed about the X1S is that it’s rocking a cadence sensor, as it’s the only one that behaves in the way that the bike displays, and if you’ve ever ridden with one of these, you know you can trick the motor into thinking you’re asking for power, even though you’re pedaling just to keep the rotation of the cranks going, without actually placing any pressure on the pedals themselves.
Considering the single-speed setup, after 20 kph or so, your pedaling doesn’t do much anymore except keep the motor engaged.
As for braking, at 25 kph (15.5 mph) an hour of max speed, these brakes are just downright mean, and it is a feature that I greatly appreciated about the bike. Sure, the treads and massive contact patch help in the mix, but I was seeing braking distances of around 4 m (12 ft) with this one, so if you ride by looking ahead, you’ll have time to stop. Discs with 180 mm diameter are found on this one.
Photo: Ovidiu Ronin / Autoevolution For night riding, the solid headlight does one heck of a job to light up your way, so no issues there, and at the rear, the taillight is definitely wide enough to be seen but doesn’t flash or shine brighter as you press the brakes.
Conclusion Now, the X1S isn’t perfect, in the sense that it’s not a bicycle designed for every rider out there, and if you have knee issues, you’ll clearly want to beg Macfox to unlock that throttle if you’re in Europe.
The throttle function is also an essential key to the puzzle for e-bikes of this style, and to see this brand really hold onto their law-abiding distribution can be considered a benefit and a drawback, depending on if you’re the rider or seller.
But, a solid frame, good components that can take a thrashing, and a price tag of $1,400 for US riders makes this one a decent option to go for, especially if you want an e-bike that can also be customized to express the color of your own soul.
Not bad there, Macfox, not bad at all.

Toyota's RAV4 PHEV Faces Software Issue That Can Disable Electric Drive
13 photos
Photo: Toyota
Currently the punchiest RAV4 that money can buy stateside, the plug-in hybrid makes up to 324 horsepower as long as the electric side of the powertrain operates without hiccups. The problem behind the latest Toyota Motor North America recall, however, starts with a controller that can take away electric propulsion due to iffy software.
When the motor-generator unit's control module fails to initialize correctly, the software may go kaput at higher speeds, leading to restricted front-drive operation. The worst-case scenario is a complete shutdown of the plug-in hybrid system. Approximately 30,978 vehicles are being recalled in the US market.
The initialization problem described by TMNA in the recall documentation occurs under certain startup conditions. Toyota further highlights that its consequences emerge when the compact-sized crossover reaches a speed that requires a compromised control mode. Warning lights instantly illuminate when the system shuts down or falls back to front-wheel drive in limp mode.
Neither outcome sounds particularly welcome, especially in a sport utility vehicle that promises up to 54 miles (87 kilometers) of all-electric range. In optimal conditions, both the internal combustion and electric sides of the powertrain come together to hit 60 miles per hour (97 kilometers per hour) in 5.4 seconds. The plug-in hybrid system relies on coordinated control of its electronics, and the recalled software can interfere with that coordination.
Per the NHTSA filing, G92A0-42460 is the part number of the motor generator's electronic control unit and inverter assembly. Supplied by Denso, this entire assembly is produced by a Japanese corporation that is partly owned by Toyota. Today, the Toyota Motor Corporation holds a 20 percent direct stake in Denso. Taking into account the entire group, Toyota owns just over 31 percent.
Photo: Toyota The largest automaker of them all by yearly sales learned about this condition after receiving a report from the Japanese market back in the summer. Warning lights had appeared during driving, and the vehicle could then operate only in FWD mode with its speed heavily restricted. The subsequent dealer inspection pointed to a communication malfunction as the rear motor generator swiches from its lower-speed control mode to high-speed control mode.
Bench tests provided the next clue, with Toyota determining that certain startup conditions prevent the rear motor-generator unit from completing initialization. When the higher-speed mode is requested, the system enters its programmed fail-safe state, increasing the risk of a crash.
Toyota then looked beyond the rear motor, for the front motor uses the same control program. By October 2026, the company had all the info required to call for a field service action. Produced in Japan, the US-market RAV4 PHEV recall population comprises 2026 models assembled between July 22, 2025, and August 19, 2026.
Through September 30, 2026, Toyota Motor North America received 58 warranty claims and 38 field technical reports from the US market. Considering that only software is to blame for this whole thing, dealers will gladly update the subject ECU software free of charge.
Customer notification letters should be mailed starting November 22, with the planned mailing period extending through December 6, 2026. Customers can check if their vehicles are potentially affected by running the VIN on the automaker's website or by using the NHTSA's lookup tool.

Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals’ siRNA candidate achieved “compelling” tau reductions in an early study of healthy volunteers, with a magnitude of effect that seems to outperform other blood-brain barrier platforms, according to Stifel.
Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals’ investigational gene silencer lowered tau protein levels in an early study, suggesting that the biotech’s approach to bypass the blood-brain barrier may be better than competing technologies.
The findings “provide important clinical validation” for Arrowhead’s platform for targeting the central nervous system through subcutaneously administered drugs, Stifel analysts said in a Wednesday note.
Results from the Phase 1/2a study, disclosed Wednesday , showed a 40% average reduction in CSF tau at day 105 in healthy volunteers who were treated with the low 2.1-mg/kg dose of the siRNA candidate, called ARO-MAPT, on days 1, 8 and 15. In those given a 6.4-mg/kg dose on the same days, CSF tau dropped by 69% on average at day 105.
Meanwhile, a 12.8-mg/kg dose of ARO-MAPT injected on days 1 and 15 triggered a mean CSF tau reduction of 73% at day 105. The maximum CSF tau reduction reached 85% in the high-dose cohort.
The early trial is actively enrolling patients, with a target of 112 participants, including healthy volunteers for the study’s first part and patients with early Alzheimer’s disease for the second portion. Wednesday’s data came from healthy volunteers.
As for safety, the primary objective of the Phase 1/2a trial, Arrowhead said that ARO-MAPT was “generally well tolerated.” Treatment-emergent adverse events were largely mild, with no serious side effects, deaths or dropouts due to toxicities.
The data, while early, could set Arrowhead up to compete against Biogen, analysts say. Both companies are advancing tau-targeting therapies that work by suppressing the expression of the MAPT gene, which codes for the tau protein.
“While details are still relatively light, the data looking compelling,” Stifel told investors in a note on Wednesday, adding that the interim findings are “arguably better than what we’ve seen with other BBB platforms.”
The firm also hinted at a potential competitive edge for Arrowhead’s subcutaneous siRNA asset, writing that the CSF tau knockdown “looks better than [Biogen’s] BIIB080,” an anti-tau antisense oligonucleotide also known as diranersen that is injected directly into the spine. ARO-MAPT, meanwhile, can be delivered via an injection under the skin.
Phase 1b data for diranersen published in 2023 showed that, across various dose levels, CSF tau declined by an average of 30% to 49% at eight weeks after the final dose of Biogen’s asset. Diranersen’s tau-lowering effect persisted through 24 weeks after the last dose, hitting an average tau reduction of up to 56%. The trial enrolled 46 patients with mild Alzheimer’s disease, and its primary endpoint was safety; CSF tau was set as a key exploratory outcome.
There have been no direct head-to-head studies between ARO-MAPT and diranersen, which prompted Jefferies to be a bit more reserved about comparing the two assets. The firm in a Wednesday note pointed to differences in study populations and dose strengths.
In May, Biogen announced that diranersen failed to meet its primary goal of showing a dose-response effect in cognitive and functional outcomes in the Phase 2 CELIA study. Nevertheless, the company detected “robust reductions in tau pathology” that were consistent with the Phase 1b study. Biogen also touted cognitive improvements and slowing of decline, especially in patients who received the lowest dose of diranersen.
Based on these efficacy signals, Biogen has decided to push diranersen into registrational development, though the company has yet to specify a timeline for this.
Arrowhead is also moving forward with ARO-MAPT, with additional healthy volunteer and Alzheimer’s disease data expected next year. Arrowhead is also in talks with health regulators to enable studies in MAPT-associated frontotemporal dementia and progressive supranuclear palsy, according to the Wednesday announcement.

Photo: © VanderWolfImages | Dreamstime.com
By Alexander Whiteman
15 October 2026
Terminals at Antwerp and Rotterdam are coming under growing pressure as unseasonably low water along the Rhine continues to restrict container barge movements on the river, with cargo being pushed towards already-constrained rail and road networks.
SeasC4U’s Gunther Ginckels told The Loadstar barges around Duisburg-Ruhrort were operating at roughly two-thirds of normal capacity, while vessels further upstream were carrying substantially smaller loads.
“Some services are suspended further upstream on the Kaub gauge, where low water has severely restricted navigation, while large volumes are being shifted to rail and truck, but alternative capacity is limited,” said Mr Ginckels.
“Cargo is still moving, but carrying capacity is sharply reduced, transport costs have risen, transit times are longer and less predictable, while inland terminals, rail networks, and trucking markets are absorbing displaced cargo at higher cost and delays.”
Some 35% of box movements along the Dutch hinterland tend to travel by inland waterway, meaning that even seeing a part of that traffic transferred to alternative modes piles massive pressure onto already constrained transport networks.
Back in August, Metro Global stated that more than 200 trucks would be required to replace lost barge capacity, and while low water levels have become part and parcel of the Rhine’s summer months in recent years, the persisting into October presented additional problems.
One source told The Loadstar : “The low waters and the additional congestion this places on rail and road infrastructure in the summer is a strain, but the with schools out and people on holiday, it is manageable. The same cannot be said for October.”
The rail operators are reportedly experiencing the biggest difficulties, with sharp increases in demand in the Rhine-Main leaving at least one intermodal operator’s train services fully booked for what Mr Ginckels said was “weeks”.
He warned that rail infrastructure was not sufficient to readily absorb all the displaced cargo, citing shortages of suitable train paths, wagons, locomotives, and drivers, and while noting that road transport offered greater flexibility, he said capacity there was also tight.
“In some affected areas, road transport is becoming the only practical alternative, because rail is already full, and even with trucks being used extensively, there is reportedly insufficient capacity for 15% to 30% of affected cargo volumes,” Mr Ginckels continued.
“Finding replacement truck capacity can take up to two weeks, while securing rail capacity may require up to six weeks’ advance notice. Even after water levels recover, logistics experts estimate it may take up to 10 days for vessel schedules to normalise.”
For terminal operators, a shift back to barges could provoke a new bout of congestion, as the arrival of delayed vessels in close succession could then create further blockages at both Rotterdam and Antwerp.
A spokesperson for the port of Rotterdam told The Loadstar it was not currently seeing any disruption to its services and that the port remained fully operational with the flow of goods continuing as normal.
“The effects are mainly visible further inland, where low water levels have a greater direct impact on the navigability of rivers and canals. That said, we see that the total volume of inland waterway transport remains reasonably stable compared with last year.”
Although sources said terminals had implemented a “one teu in, one teu out” policy for the barges and trains making their way to the terminals with containers, demanding they take away an equivalent number to those discharged.
This condition of discharge is reportedly applicable for full and empty containers, but sources say the restriction is only complicating container flows and adding to barge waiting times – although neither Antwerp nor Rotterdam had yet to confirm the rule to The Loadstar.
Mr Ginckels said the situation was now “one of the most serious Rhine navigation disruptions since the historic low-water events of 2018″.
“The strongest effects are those being felt down in southern Germany, Switzerland, and the Upper Rhine corridor.”

BMW Shenyang Plant Now Produces Gen6 Electric Vehicle Batteries
12 photos
Photo: BMW
The Bavarian automaker that gave us the 3.0 CSL and the M1 has kicked off sixth-generation battery production at the Shenyang complex in China. Obviously enough, the packs assembled there will go into electric models assembled in China for mostly the Chinese market. Shenyang joins two additional Gen6 battery plants, with both of them located in Europe.
BMW describes the strategy as "local for local," and it's easy to understand why. The Chinese plant supplies Neue Klasse battery-electric models built in China, including the long-wheelbase version of the iX3, cutting transport distances and keeping the supply chain tight in the process. The first vehicles to use these batteries are the localized iX3 L and i3 L.
In addition to a few additional inches of wheelbase, BMW also changed software and hardware. In both cases, the most obvious hardware-related modification is the switch from pop-out flush exterior door handles to semi-recessed pull handles. The more conventional handles were prompted by China's mandatory standard GB 48001-2026, which bans a number of problematic designs.
That being cleared up, we also have to highlight that BMW uses Gen6 cylindrical battery cells in the facelifted i7. The full-electric version of the i7 uses the Cluster Architecture, and by extension, BMW paired the latest cell technology with the Gen5 module design. The i7's 4695 cells hold 20 percent more energy by volume than the fifth-generation prismatic battery cells.
Neue Klasse models like the iX3, iX4, and i3 do not group cylindrical cells into modules before placing them in a battery housing. Instead, the Bavarian automaker puts them directly into the battery enclosure, eliminating the module design altogether. That frees up space while also reducing parts, allowing BMW to shape the pack more freely.
Photo: BMW BMW China uses EVE and CATL battery cells in 4695 and 46120 flavors. These formats are meant for sedans and SUVs, respectively. Going the Gen6 route also enabled 30 percent faster charging on DC and up to 30 percent more driving range, depending on application.
Mounted on the high-voltage battery, the so-called Energy Master should be viewed as one central unit that manages energy flow, charging, thermal behavior, and battery health, consolidating functions that would otherwise be distributed across multiple control units. Manufacturing follows a very precise sequence, with BMW China first inspecting each cell before joining them with the cooling units.
The resulting clusters are then cleaned and welded to the cell-contact system. A foaming process then bonds the assembly, after which Shenyang workers close, seal, and rivet the housing. The Energy Master is installed right after that. Every pack then undergoes a complete end-of-line test for everything imaginable, with BMW monitoring laser-welded joints in real time for added peace of mind.
Among others, artificial intelligence is used to catch deviations early. Those systems don't make the Neue Klasse-specific packs inherently better, yet reduce the chance that a defect reaches customer vehicles. Beyond these facilities, Gen6 battery production will soon be handled by two additional plants in the United States and Mexico.

PERTH, Australia — Imagine an unmanned ground vehicle large enough to cart a 20-foot container around the battlefield, as well as possessing sufficient power to run a radar or launch a barrage of missiles.
Thales Australia says it has built just such a robot.
The company unveiled its BladeHaul extra-large, heavy-duty UGV on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition being held in Perth, Western Australia.
Looking something akin to an aircraft tug, the BladeHaul relies on the chassis and driveline of Thales Australia’s popular Bushmaster 4x4 protected mobility vehicle that is in widespread Australian Army use.
According to its designer, this uncrewed vehicle “is engineered to outperform all existing and planned counterparts in payload capacity and operational flexibility.”
Official specs list a payload capacity of 10-plus tons for this cargo UGV, and a driving range comparable to that of the Bushmaster’s 600-plus kilometers.
The Bushmaster’s original mechanicals have been replaced by a hybrid energy and battery storage solution from 3ME Technology, Thales Australia’s partner in the effort.
3ME Technology has extensive experience in the mining sector, and it previously developed a hybrid-engined Bushmaster vehicle.
Thales Australia and 3ME Technologies unveiled the BladeHaul UGV at Land Forces 2026 in Perth, Western Australia, in October. (Gordon Arthur)
For the BladeHaul the company has assembled a 660V power system that offers 110kWh of power.
Justin Bain, CEO of 3ME Technology, said: “Working with Thales Australia brings together the best of Australian innovation, combining 3ME Technology’s systems engineering and platform development capabilities with the Bushmaster’s proven performance and established manufacturing base. Together we’re delivering an entirely new XL-UGV at a time when demand for contested logistics and remote power solutions for littoral environments is present and growing.”
Thales Australia envisages three potential use cases for the BladeHaul: as a cargo mover in zones of contested logistics; as a mobile and enduring power source for other equipment; and as a highly mobile platform for sensors and effectors.
The vehicle could therefore find utility in tasks such as carrying coastal anti-ship missiles, as a counter-drone system, mounting an air surveillance radar, reloading munitions or detecting mines. For the latter mission, it could have a mine plow or rollers mounted on the front.
The manufacturer says the vehicle’s applications are limited only by the imagination of the user. For example, it could carry containerized missile systems or launch drone swarms, one official told Defense News.
Alternatively, it could generate and supply power for a field hospital, a command post or simply act as a standalone generator. It offers a 1MW of power. To put that in perspective, 1MW could simultaneously power 1,000 homes.
To add to its versatility, the BladeHaul 4x4 UGV can fit in transport aircraft like the C-130 and A400M.
The BladeHaul is not yet ready for action, however. Work on the project began 18 months ago, with progress really accelerating over the past six months, but it does not yet have a working autonomy system.
Thales Australia signed a memorandum of understanding with Deakin University at Land Forces 2026 to develop its autonomy suite. This will build upon the suite used on the smaller Guardian Angel UGV unveiled by Thales earlier this year. It will be capable of remote, fully autonomous or follow-me operations, for example.
Thales Australia said in a statement: “By integrating advanced autonomy that enables human-machine teaming, hybrid technology, heavy payload capacity and power generation within a single platform, Thales Australia and 3ME Technology are delivering a next-generation solution that enhances operational readiness and supports Australia’s commitment to sovereign defense innovation.”
The BladeHaul is aimed at the Australian Army, but its appeal extends to any land force, according to the manufacturer.
The vehicle has no V-shaped hull to protect against underbody blasts, as there is no crew aboard. However, ballistic protection could be added to it depending on the function.
Bain said there is interest in a UGV version able to carry a 40-foot container too. “If there’s sufficient demand, we may look at that.”
